title: Breathing and finding food: how animal bodies do it

summary.text: This unit is about two jobs every animal body must do. It must get air, and it must find food. Every part of an animal's body needs oxygen, a gas in air and water. Animals take it in with lungs, with gills, or straight through damp skin. Insects even have tiny air pipes all over their bodies. Animals find food with their senses: smell, sight, hearing, touch, and some senses we do not have at all, like a bat's echo-hearing. Scientists understand breathing well. They still argue about how lungs first appeared, and why earthworms crawl out when it rains.
summary.art: A split picture: on the left a child breathing out a little cloud onto a cold steel tumbler, a fish with red gills and a frog with shiny wet skin. On the right, a dog sniffing, a bat sending out sound waves and an ant on a sugar trail.

intro.hook: Try this. Hold a cold steel tumbler close to your mouth. Breathe out on it slowly, three times. What appears on the steel? Now look at a fish in a tank. It never comes up for air. How is it breathing?
intro.text: In the summer, when village ponds in Bengal and Assam dry up, people sometimes dig in the hard mud. And there, in the mud, they find fish. Some are still alive, days after the water has gone. One of them, the climbing perch, can even wriggle across wet grass to the next pond. A fish that lives without water? How does it get its air? And how does any animal, in water, mud or sky, find enough to eat? This unit is about those two jobs: breathing and finding food.
intro.art: A cracked dry pond bed at dawn, a village child kneeling and holding up a small greenish fish from a hole in the mud, a fresh pond shining in the distance.

outcomes: I can say why every animal needs oxygen: every part of its body uses oxygen to get energy from food.
I can explain how lungs, gills and skin each take in oxygen, and why all of them are thin, damp and close to blood.
I can count and compare my breaths before and after exercise, as a fair test, and say what the numbers show.
I can show that breathed-out air is different from room air, using a chuna water test.
I can name the senses animals use to find food, including senses people do not have, like echo-hearing and heat-sensing.
I can describe different ways animals get food: grazing, hunting, waiting, filtering, trapping and scavenging.
I can say what scientists agree about breathing, and what they still argue about.
I can explain big ideas: the oxygen I breathe was made by plants and tiny sea algae, and every cell in me breathes.

terms.meaning: A gas with no colour and no smell. It is in air, and a little of it is mixed into water. Animals need it to stay alive.
terms.example: Each time you breathe in, oxygen goes into your body.
terms.art: Air drawn as tiny dots, with a few dots coloured blue and labelled oxygen, flowing into a child's nose.

terms.meaning: A gas our bodies make and breathe out. Plants take it in and use it to make food.
terms.example: The fizz in a soda drink is carbon dioxide. You breathe out a little carbon dioxide all the time.
terms.art: A child breathing out grey dots towards a tulsi plant, which is drinking them in.

terms.meaning: Moving air or water in and out of the body, so that oxygen can get in and carbon dioxide can get out.
terms.example: Your chest rises when you breathe in, and falls when you breathe out.
terms.art: A child with a hand on the chest, the chest rising with an arrow up.

terms.meaning: What happens inside every cell: the cell uses oxygen to unlock the energy stored in food. Breathing feeds respiration.
terms.example: When you run, your leg cells do more respiration, so you breathe faster.
terms.art: A zoomed-in circle on a leg muscle showing a cell taking in oxygen and food and giving out a spark of energy.

terms.meaning: The tiny living unit that bodies are built from. Your body has many millions of millions of cells.
terms.example: Your skin, blood and muscles are all made of cells.
terms.art: A child's arm with a magnifying circle showing cells like small bricks.

terms.meaning: Two soft, spongy bags inside the chest. Air goes in and out of them. Oxygen passes from the lungs into the blood.
terms.example: People, dogs, crows, snakes and dolphins all have lungs.
terms.art: A simple drawing of two pink lungs in a child's chest, with the windpipe branching like a tree.

terms.meaning: Millions of tiny bubbles at the ends of the branches inside the lungs. Their walls are thinner than tissue paper. Oxygen passes through them into the blood.
terms.example: Your two lungs hold about 480 million air sacs, like a huge bunch of tiny grapes.
terms.art: A branch of the lung ending in a bunch of grape-like bubbles, each wrapped in red blood vessels.

terms.meaning: Feathery red parts on each side of a fish's head. Water flows over them, and they take oxygen out of the water.
terms.example: At a fish market, sellers lift the flap on a fish's head to show its bright red gills.
terms.art: A rohu fish with its gill flap lifted, showing rows of red feathery gills, and arrows of water flowing in at the mouth and out under the flap.

terms.meaning: The hard flap that covers a fish's gills. It opens and closes as water flows out.
terms.example: Watch a goldfish closely. The flaps behind its eyes open and shut all the time.
terms.art: A goldfish side-on with its gill cover slightly open.

terms.meaning: Taking in oxygen straight through the skin. It only works if the skin is thin and kept damp.
terms.example: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. It breathes only through its damp skin.
terms.art: An earthworm on damp soil with tiny blue dots passing into its skin.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes along the sides of an insect's body. Air goes in through them, into thin pipes that reach every part of the insect.
terms.example: A grasshopper has a row of spiracles along each side.
terms.art: A grasshopper close up, with a row of small dots along its side, and thin tubes branching inside.

terms.meaning: The nostril on top of the head of a dolphin or a whale. It breathes air through it at the surface.
terms.example: The Ganges river dolphin comes up to breathe through its blowhole every minute or two.
terms.art: A Ganges river dolphin breaking the brown river surface, a small puff of spray rising from its blowhole.

terms.meaning: The ways a body learns about the world: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching. Some animals have extra senses.
terms.example: A dog finds a hidden biscuit by smell.
terms.art: A dog with its nose to the ground, following a dotted smell trail to a biscuit under a cushion.

terms.meaning: Finding things by sending out sounds and listening for the echoes that bounce back.
terms.example: Bats and dolphins find insects and fish in the dark this way.
terms.art: A bat at dusk sending out curved sound lines that bounce off a moth and come back to its ears.

terms.meaning: An animal that hunts and eats other animals.
terms.example: A kingfisher is a predator. It dives to catch small fish.
terms.art: A kingfisher diving into a pond towards a small fish.

terms.meaning: An animal that is hunted and eaten by another animal.
terms.example: A small fish is the kingfisher's prey.
terms.art: A small silver fish darting away from a kingfisher's shadow.

terms.meaning: An animal that sieves tiny bits of food out of water.
terms.example: Flamingos sieve tiny shrimps and algae out of lake water with their beaks.
terms.art: A pink flamingo with its head upside down in shallow water, its beak working like a sieve.

terms.meaning: An animal that eats the bodies of animals that have already died.
terms.example: Vultures and crows are scavengers. They clean up dead animals.
terms.art: Two vultures on a dry field near a cow skeleton, a crow waiting nearby.

terms.meaning: Tiny plant-like living things that live in water. Like plants, they make food from sunlight and give out oxygen.
terms.example: The green colour in an old bucket of water is algae.
terms.art: A drop of pond water under a magnifier showing tiny green specks and threads.

explanations.definition: Every cell in an animal's body uses oxygen to unlock the energy stored in food. This is called respiration. Breathing is how the body gets that oxygen in.
explanations.description: Food is like stored energy, a bit like wood waiting to be burned. To get the energy out, a cell needs oxygen, just as a fire needs air. The cell joins the food and oxygen together slowly and gently. Out comes energy to move, grow, think and keep warm. Out also comes carbon dioxide and a little water, which the body must get rid of. So breathing has two jobs. It brings oxygen in. It takes carbon dioxide out. A cell that gets no oxygen soon stops working. That is why we cannot hold our breath for very long.
examples: When you run, your leg muscles use more oxygen, so you breathe faster.
A candle under an upturned glass goes out when the oxygen runs low. Cells use oxygen too, but slowly, without flames.
A sleeping dog breathes slowly. A dog that has just chased a ball pants.
explanations.art: A cell drawn as a little factory with doors: food and oxygen go in, energy sparks, carbon dioxide and water come out.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea behind all breathing: why animals need oxygen at all.

explanations.concept: What every breathing part has in common
explanations.definition: Lungs, gills and breathing skin all do the same job in the same way. They are thin, they are damp, they are very big for their size, and they have blood flowing just underneath.
explanations.description: Oxygen can only get into the body by passing through a thin, wet wall. On the other side of that wall is blood, which carries the oxygen away to every cell. So the best breathing parts have very thin walls. They stay damp, because oxygen has to dissolve in a film of water before it can pass through. They are folded or branched many times, so there is lots of surface. More surface lets more oxygen in at once. And blood is always flowing right next to them. Lungs, gills and frog skin look very different. But zoom in and they are the same trick.
examples: Your lungs are folded into about 480 million tiny air sacs. Spread flat, they would cover about a badminton court.
A fish's gills are split into hundreds of thin, feathery threads.
A frog's skin is thin and slimy, with many tiny blood vessels underneath.
explanations.art: Three zoomed-in circles side by side: a lung air sac, a gill thread and frog skin, each a thin wall with oxygen dots passing into red blood underneath.
explanations.context: This card shows how lungs, gills and breathing skin are really the same idea underneath.

explanations.definition: Lungs are two spongy bags in the chest. A sheet of muscle under them, the diaphragm, pulls down to suck air in, and relaxes to let air out.
explanations.description: Air goes in through your nose or mouth and down a pipe called the windpipe. The windpipe splits into two, one branch for each lung. Each branch splits again and again, like the branches of a banyan tree. At the very tips are tiny air sacs. Oxygen passes through their thin walls into the blood. Carbon dioxide passes the other way, out of the blood into the air sacs. Then you breathe it out. Your lungs cannot move by themselves. The diaphragm, a dome of muscle under them, pulls down and makes space. Air rushes in to fill it. Breathed-out air still has some oxygen in it, but less than room air, and much more carbon dioxide.
examples: People, cows, crows, snakes, tortoises and dolphins all breathe with lungs.
A dolphin's lungs fill through a blowhole on top of its head.
Room air is about 21 parts in 100 oxygen. Breathed-out air is about 16 parts in 100. Your body kept the rest.
explanations.art: A child's body outline with the windpipe branching into two lungs like an upside-down tree, and a dome-shaped diaphragm below, with arrows showing it pull down.
explanations.context: This card explains how lungs work, from the nose to the tiny air sacs.

explanations.definition: Gills take oxygen out of water. A fish gulps water in through its mouth. The water flows over the gills and out under the gill covers.
explanations.description: Water holds far less oxygen than air, about thirty times less in the same space. So a fish must be very good at catching it. Its gills are rows of thin red threads, each covered in even thinner folds. Blood flows through them the opposite way to the water. This clever trick means the blood keeps meeting water that has more oxygen than it does. Fish can take most of the oxygen out of the water that passes over them. Out of water, the soft gill threads stick together and dry out, like a wet paintbrush pulled out of a jar. Then there is too little surface, and the fish cannot breathe. That is why most fish die in air, even though air has more oxygen than water.
examples: Rohu, catla and goldfish breathe with gills.
Tadpoles breathe with gills. Most grow lungs when they become frogs.
Crabs and prawns breathe with gills too, tucked under their hard shells.
explanations.art: A fish's head cut away to show water arrows flowing in at the mouth, over red gill threads, and out under the gill cover, with blood arrows going the other way.
explanations.context: This card explains how fish take oxygen out of water with their gills.

explanations.definition: Some animals take in oxygen straight through their skin. Their skin must be thin and kept damp, or the oxygen cannot pass through.
explanations.description: An earthworm has no lungs and no gills. Oxygen from the air between soil crumbs passes straight through its moist skin into its blood. If an earthworm dries out in the sun, it can no longer breathe. Frogs have lungs, but they also breathe through their skin. A frog resting underwater in a pond in winter can get all the oxygen it needs through its skin. Some salamanders, a group of animals related to frogs, have no lungs at all. In 2008 scientists found the first frog known to have no lungs. It lives in cold, fast streams in Borneo. Fast, cold water holds plenty of oxygen, so its skin is enough.
examples: An earthworm breathes only through its skin.
A frog breathes with lungs and with its skin.
Mudskippers, the fish that hop on the mud in Indian mangroves, take in oxygen through their skin and the inside of their mouths.
explanations.art: An earthworm in a cross-section of damp soil, a frog half in a pond, and a flat-headed frog in a rushing stream, each with small oxygen dots passing into the skin.
explanations.context: This card explains animals that breathe through their skin, like earthworms and frogs.

explanations.definition: Insects breathe through holes in their sides called spiracles, and air pipes that reach every cell. Some fish can breathe air as well as water.
explanations.description: An insect has no lungs. Air goes in through small holes along its sides. It travels down thin pipes that branch and branch until they reach every tiny part of the body. So in an insect, air goes straight to the cells. Some fish live in warm, muddy ponds where the water has little oxygen. The climbing perch, called koi in Bengali, has an extra breathing room above its gills, folded like a maze. It gulps air at the surface. It can stay alive out of water for hours if it stays damp. The magur and singhi catfish sold alive in Indian markets can also breathe air. That is why they stay alive in a bucket with very little water.
examples: A grasshopper breathes through spiracles along its sides.
A mosquito young lives in water but breathes air through a tiny tube it pokes up through the surface.
The climbing perch can wriggle across wet grass from one pond to another.
explanations.art: A grasshopper with its air pipes drawn like branching silver threads, next to a climbing perch with a maze-like breathing room above its gills, gulping air at a pond's surface.
explanations.context: This card shows more ways animals breathe: insects' air pipes and fish that gulp air.

explanations.definition: Animals that breathe air but hunt underwater must hold their breath. Animals that fly very high must get oxygen from thin air.
explanations.description: Dolphins, whales, turtles and otters breathe with lungs, so they must come up for air. The Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal, comes up every minute or two. Some deep-diving whales can stay under for more than an hour. One Cuvier's beaked whale was recorded staying under for 222 minutes, nearly four hours. They store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles, and slow their hearts while they dive. High in the sky, the air is thin, so each breath has less oxygen. Bar-headed geese fly right over the Himalayas to spend the winter in India. Their lungs, blood and hearts are extra good at grabbing oxygen.
examples: A Ganges river dolphin surfaces every minute or two to breathe.
A sea turtle can sleep underwater for hours, because a resting body uses little oxygen.
Bar-headed geese cross the Himalayas twice a year.
explanations.art: A Ganges river dolphin surfacing in a brown river, and high above the snowy Himalayas a V of bar-headed geese.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that hold their breath for a long time, or breathe very thin air.

explanations.concept: How animals find food: their senses
explanations.definition: Animals find food with their senses. Different animals rely on different senses, depending on where and how they live.
explanations.description: A dog finds food mostly by smell. Its nose has many times more smell cells than yours. An eagle finds food mostly by sight, spotting a mouse from high in the sky. An owl can catch a mouse in the dark just by hearing its rustle. A cat's whiskers feel tiny movements of air, which helps it in the dark. Some animals have senses we do not have at all. Bats and Ganges river dolphins send out clicks and listen to the echoes. Sharks feel the tiny electricity made by the muscles of hidden fish. Pit vipers, like the Malabar pit viper of the Western Ghats, have pits on their faces that sense the warmth of a mouse in the dark.
examples: Ants find food by smell, and leave a smell trail for other ants to follow.
A mosquito finds you by the carbon dioxide you breathe out, and by your warmth.
A honeybee sees colours on flowers that we cannot see.
explanations.art: A row of animals each with one glowing sense: a dog's nose, an eagle's eye, an owl's ears, a cat's whiskers, a bat's sound waves and a snake's heat pits.
explanations.context: This card explains how animals use their senses to find food.

explanations.definition: Animals get food in many different ways. Some graze, some hunt, some wait, some sieve, some build traps and some clean up the dead.
explanations.description: A cow grazes. It walks slowly and eats grass for hours. A cheetah hunts. It chases its prey at great speed. A crocodile waits. It lies still in the river until an animal comes close. A flamingo filters. It sieves tiny shrimps and algae out of lake water. A spider builds a trap. Its sticky web catches flying insects. A vulture scavenges. It eats animals that have already died, and keeps the land clean. Each way of eating goes with a body that fits it. A cow has flat teeth for grinding. A cheetah has long legs and sharp claws. A flamingo has a beak like a sieve.
examples: A hummingbird or a sunbird sips nectar with a long, thin beak.
A whale shark, the biggest fish, filters tiny food out of seawater.
An antlion digs a pit in dry sand and waits at the bottom for ants to fall in.
explanations.art: Six small scenes in a grid: a cow grazing, a cheetah running, a crocodile waiting, a flamingo filtering, a spider's web and a vulture.
explanations.context: This card explains the different ways animals get their food.

explanations.concept: Smell may be the oldest sense
explanations.description: Long before there were eyes or ears, the first living things were single cells floating in water. Even today, bacteria can swim towards sugar and away from harmful things. They do it by sensing chemicals, which is a kind of smelling. So many scientists think that sensing chemicals is the oldest way of finding food. Smell and taste may be the great-grandparents of all the senses. This is a good idea with lots of evidence, but nobody was there to watch, so we call it an idea.
examples: Bacteria swim towards a drop of sugar under a microscope.
A tiny single-celled creature in pond water turns towards food.
Ants and termites still use smell to find food and talk to each other.
explanations.art: A drop of water under a microscope with tiny bacteria all swimming towards a sugar crystal at one side.
explanations.context: This card shares an idea about the very first way living things found food.

explanations.description: Long ago, all animals with backbones lived in water and breathed with gills. Some fish lived in warm, muddy swamps with little oxygen. They began to gulp air into a pouch in their throats. Over a very long time, these pouches became lungs. Many fish today have a gas bag instead, called a swim bladder, which helps them float. Which came first, the lung or the swim bladder? Scientists have argued about this.
examples: Lungfish, which still live in Africa, South America and Australia, have lungs and gills.
A goldfish has a swim bladder. It helps it float without sinking or rising.
Bichirs, an old kind of African fish, have simple lungs.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin, in his book On the Origin of Species (1859)
perspectives.explanation: Darwin thought the swim bladder of fish came first, and slowly changed into the lungs of land animals.

Studies of old kinds of fish, like bichirs and lungfish, and of fossils, suggest the opposite. Lungs came first, in early fish. Later, in many fish, the lung changed into a swim bladder for floating. Most scientists now lean this way, but the details are still being studied.

explanations.art: A muddy ancient swamp with a fish poking its mouth above the water to gulp air, and a cut-away of its throat showing a small air pouch.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle: did lungs come from fish swim bladders, or the other way round?

explanations.concept: Why do earthworms come out when it rains?
explanations.description: After heavy rain, you often see earthworms lying on paths and roads. Earthworms breathe through their skin, so many people think they come up to stop drowning. But earthworms can live for a long time in water that has oxygen in it. So scientists are not sure. There are several ideas, and maybe more than one is true.
examples: Earthworms on a wet road in the monsoon.
An earthworm in a jar of tap water can live for days.
Some fishermen in other countries drum on the ground to call worms up.

perspectives.explanation: Water soaking the soil may hold less oxygen than air did. The worms come up to breathe more easily.
When everything is wet, worms can crawl far over the surface without drying out. Rain is a good time to move to a new place.
The drumming of rain may feel like the digging of a mole, which eats worms. The worms crawl up to escape it. People who drum on the ground to call worms up support this idea.

explanations.art: A wet path in the monsoon with several earthworms on it, and three thought bubbles above them: a bubble, a road, and a mole.
explanations.context: This card is about a puzzle nobody has fully solved: why earthworms crawl out after rain.

agreed.text: All animals need oxygen, and they all give out carbon dioxide.
agreed.evidence: Animals kept in a sealed box with no fresh air soon struggle. Scientists can measure the oxygen going in and the carbon dioxide coming out of any animal, from a mouse to a beetle.

agreed.text: Lungs, gills and breathing skin all work the same way: oxygen passes through a thin, damp wall into blood.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, the walls of air sacs, gill threads and frog skin are all very thin, with tiny blood vessels right underneath.

agreed.text: Breathed-out air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than room air.
agreed.evidence: Chuna water, which is limewater, turns milky with carbon dioxide. It turns milky fast with breathed-out air, and very slowly with room air. Gas meters in hospitals measure the same thing.

agreed.text: Animals breathe faster when they are active, because their muscles use more oxygen.
agreed.evidence: Count anyone's breaths before and after running, and you get the same pattern. Doctors use this in fitness tests.

agreed.text: Animals find food with their senses, and different animals rely on different senses.
agreed.evidence: Experiments show that bats with their ears blocked crash into things, while dogs can follow a smell trail that is days old.

agreed.text: The oxygen in air was made by living things: plants on land and tiny algae in the sea.
agreed.evidence: Ancient rocks show that there was almost no oxygen in the air until tiny ocean living things began to make it, more than two billion years ago.

challenging.who: A common idea among young children, and some adults
challenging.for: Fish never come up for air, and we cannot see them breathing.
challenging.against: Fish breathe all the time. Watch a fish in a tank. Its mouth and gill covers open and shut, pumping water over the gills. The gills take oxygen out of the water.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that fish do not need to breathe.

challenging.claim: We breathe in oxygen and breathe out only carbon dioxide.
challenging.who: A common way of saying it, even in some books
challenging.for: It is a simple way to remember breathing.
challenging.against: Breathed-out air still has plenty of oxygen, about 16 parts in 100, compared with 21 parts in room air. That is why the kiss of life, when a person breathes into someone who has stopped breathing, can work. We breathe out a little extra carbon dioxide and water, not only carbon dioxide.
challenging.context: This card is about a common way of describing breathing, and why it is not quite right.

challenging.who: An old saying, as blind as a bat
challenging.for: Bats fly at night, and many have small eyes.
challenging.against: Bats can see. Many fruit bats see very well. Insect-eating bats also use echolocation. In the 1790s, an Italian scientist, Lazzaro Spallanzani, found that bats could still fly in the dark with their eyes covered. A Swiss surgeon, Louis Jurine, then found that bats lost their way when their ears were blocked. In the 1930s and 1940s, Donald Griffin and Robert Galambos showed that bats use sounds too high for us to hear.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that bats are blind, and how scientists found out the truth.

challenging.claim: Whales and dolphins are fish, because they live in water.
challenging.who: A common idea, and an old way of sorting animals
challenging.for: They live in water and have fish-like shapes.
challenging.against: Whales and dolphins breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole. They would drown if they could not reach the surface. Their babies drink milk. Living in water is not the same as breathing water.
challenging.context: This card is about whether dolphins and whales breathe like fish.

challenging.who: Lieutenant Daldorff, a Danish officer at Tranquebar in Tamil Nadu, who wrote in the 1790s that he saw one high in a palm tree
challenging.for: The fish can breathe air and wriggle across land. Its scientific name, Anabas, means 'one who climbs'.
challenging.against: Nobody has seen it climb a tree since. Many scientists think birds like kites and crows caught the fish, carried them to trees and dropped them. Because the fish breathes air, it could still be alive up there, which made it look like a climber.
challenging.context: This card is about an old report that a fish climbed a palm tree, and what scientists think now.

challenging.claim: Every cell in your body is partly made of tiny ancient bacteria.
challenging.who: Lynn Margulis, an American biologist, in 1967. Her paper was turned down by many journals before it was published.
challenging.for: The tiny energy parts inside our cells, called mitochondria, use oxygen just like some bacteria do. They even have their own little bit of DNA, like bacteria.
challenging.against: At first, most biologists thought the idea was strange and unlikely. But DNA tests later showed that mitochondria really did come from bacteria that moved into bigger cells long ago.
challenging.context: This card is about a once-mocked idea about where our cells' breathing parts came from.

big_questions.q: If a fish has gills that take oxygen from water, why does it die in air, which has much more oxygen?
big_questions.hint: Think of a wet paintbrush taken out of water. What happens to its soft hairs?

big_questions.q: Where was the oxygen in your last breath a week ago?
big_questions.hint: Who puts oxygen into the air? Think of trees, grass and the green stuff in ponds and seas.

big_questions.q: If every cell in you breathes, which part of you is really doing the breathing: your nose, your lungs or you?
big_questions.hint: Your nose and lungs are like doors. Where does the oxygen finally go?

big_questions.q: A dog smells a world we cannot smell. A bat hears echoes we cannot hear. Is the world we see the whole world?
big_questions.hint: Think of all the senses other animals have that we do not.

big_questions.q: Plants breathe out oxygen, and we breathe out carbon dioxide that plants take in. Are we and the trees really separate?
big_questions.hint: Where does your breath go after it leaves you?

big_questions.q: Is it fair for one animal to eat another?
big_questions.hint: What would happen to the forest if there were no hunters at all? What if there were no vultures?

big_questions.q: Why does breathing slowly make you feel calm?
big_questions.hint: Try it. Breathe in for four counts, out for six. What changes in your body?

big_questions.q: Could an animal live on a planet with no oxygen at all?
big_questions.hint: Some tiny living things on Earth live where there is no oxygen. How might they get energy?

big_questions.q: Why did different animals end up with lungs, gills or breathing skin, instead of all having the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each one lives: dry land, water or damp soil.

big_questions.q: Should people keep fish in small bowls, or birds in cages?
big_questions.hint: What does a fish need to breathe well? What does a bird need to find its food?

story.title: The Fish in the Palm Tree
story.note: Tranquebar (now Tharangambadi, in Tamil Nadu) was a Danish trading town. A Danish officer, Lieutenant Daldorff, really did report in the 1790s that he saw a climbing perch high on a palmyra palm there, and the fish was named after his report. Selvi, her grandmother and everything they say and do are imagined. The science of how the fish breathes is real.
text: The summer the tank dried, Selvi learned to hear fish breathing.

She was nine. She lived in Tranquebar, a town by the sea where the Danish ships came in, and where the white fort sat on the sand like a sleeping cow. Behind her house was the village tank, a square pond with stone steps going down. In March it was full of water lilies. By May it was a brown puddle. By June it was cracked mud, hard as a roof tile.

Every evening her grandmother, Paati, took a short digging stick and went down the steps. Selvi followed with a clay pot. Paati knelt on the cracked mud and tapped it, the way you tap a coconut to hear if it is ripe. Where it sounded soft, she dug. And there, a hand deep in the mud, there were fish.

They were small and greenish, as long as Selvi's hand, with spiny fins and a dark spot near the tail. They were alive. They had been living in that mud for days, with no water at all. Paati dropped them into the pot with a fistful of wet mud and some wet leaves, and nothing else.
'You will kill them,' Selvi said the first time. 'Fish need water.'
'Not these,' said Paati. 'Put your ear to the pot.'
Selvi did. At first she heard nothing. Then, very softly, she heard it. A little click. A tiny wet gulp. Then another.
'They are breathing,' said Paati. 'They drink the air, like you and me. Just keep them damp. If they dry out, they die. If they stay damp, they live.'
Selvi did not understand it. She just remembered it, the way you remember a song.
That was the summer the Danish officer came walking through the palms.

He was a tall man with a red face and a notebook. The children called him the leaf man, because he picked up leaves, beetles, shells and stones, and wrote about every one. The grown-ups said he was a lieutenant at the fort. He spoke a little Tamil, badly and politely. Mostly he pointed.

One afternoon, after the first thunderstorm of the year, Selvi was sitting under the palmyra palms near the tank. The air smelled of wet dust. Above her, a black kite was circling. It dipped low over the puddles in the tank, came up with something silver in its claws, and flapped heavily to the top of the nearest palm. There it sat, tearing at its catch. Then a crow came. The kite and the crow screamed at each other. Something fell out of the kite's claws and tumbled down into the rough, cracked bark of the trunk.
Selvi stood up to look. Just then the leaf man came round the corner.

He saw it at once. A fish, wriggling in a cleft of the palm bark, as high as a man's shoulder. Its spiny gill covers were hooked into the bark. Its tail was flicking. It looked exactly as though it was climbing up.

The leaf man made a sound Selvi had never heard a grown man make. It was half a gasp and half a laugh. He took out his notebook. He looked at the fish, then wrote, then looked again. He measured the height with his hand. 'Climbing!' he said in his own language, and then in Tamil, 'It goes up! The fish goes up the tree!'
Selvi opened her mouth to tell him about the kite. But he was talking fast, to himself, and he did not look at her.

He lifted the fish carefully from the bark. He looked worried now. He held it out in the bright, dry air and shook his head. 'It will die,' he said. 'No water. It will die.' He reached into his bag for a glass jar, the kind he kept beetles in, full of strong-smelling spirit. That was what he did with things he found. He kept them dead and still, so he could study them later.
And Selvi understood, all at once, what Paati had been telling her all summer.

'No,' she said. 'Wait.' She ran to her house and came back with the clay pot, the one with wet mud and wet leaves at the bottom. She held it out. He looked at her, then at the pot. Then, slowly, he put the fish in.

Selvi sprinkled water from her hands over the leaves. She did not fill the pot. The fish lay still, then wriggled down into the wet leaves. Then it came up and opened its mouth at the top of the pot, and took a gulp of air. Click. Then another.
The leaf man knelt down in the dust. He put his ear to the pot, the way Selvi had done.
'It breathes the air,' Selvi said in Tamil, slowly, so he would understand. 'Not only water. Keep it damp, and it lives. Paati finds them in the dry tank every day.'

He listened for a long time. Then he looked up at the top of the palm, where the kite had gone. Selvi pointed at the sky, flapped her arms like a kite, opened her fingers and let an invisible fish drop. He watched her. She could not tell if he believed her.

He kept the fish alive in the pot for six days. Every evening Selvi came to sprinkle it, and every evening it gulped its little gulps of air. He drew it many times. He wrote pages and pages. Then the rains came properly, and the tank began to fill, and Selvi carried the pot down the stone steps and tipped the fish into the brown water.
It sank. Then it rose. At the surface, it took one more bubble of air, and was gone.

Years later, Selvi heard that the leaf man had sent his writing across the sea, to the scientists in England. In their books, the little fish was given a name that meant the climber. Nobody wrote down a girl, a pot of wet mud, or a kite.
Selvi did not mind very much. On summer evenings, she still went down the steps of the dry tank with a digging stick, and knelt, and tapped, and listened for the click.
story.epiphany: The climbing perch was alive in the palm tree because it breathes air as well as water. As long as its body stays damp, it can live out of water for hours. So the fish did not have to climb to get up there. A bird could have dropped it, and it would still be alive.
ask: Why did Paati keep the fish in wet mud and wet leaves, and not in a pot full of water?
The leaf man thought the fish would die in air. Why do most fish die in air?
What did Selvi see that the leaf man did not? Why do you think he did not write it down?
How could you test whether a fish really climbs trees, or is dropped by birds?

rules: Cut out the animal cards and the bonus cards. Shuffle the animal cards and put them face down.

Put it on the mat that shows how it breathes, and say one reason. Some animals use two ways. Then put the card between two mats.
A right mat with a good reason wins one breath token. If someone thinks it is wrong, check the answer list together.
After every fifth card, turn over a bonus card. The first player to act out how that animal finds food wins two tokens.

flow.say: Every animal needs oxygen. But they get it in different ways: lungs, gills, damp skin, or tiny air pipes. Let's sort animals by how they breathe.

flow.do: Play the card 'Frog' together as a practice round.

flow.kid: Practice card: frog. Which mat? It might be two!

check.q: Practice card: frog. Where does it go?
options: Between LUNGS and SKIN
GILLS only
AIR PIPES
check.why: A grown frog breathes with lungs, and also through its thin, damp skin. That's why frogs stay near water. Picking 'gills' is half right for a young frog: a tadpole has gills. Once it grows up, most frogs breathe with lungs and skin.

flow.context: This is a practice round in Lungs, Gills or Skin? You decide where the frog card goes.

flow.do: Take turns until all cards are played. After every fifth card, turn over a bonus card. Use the answer list in the parent note when anyone disagrees.

flow.kid: Take a card. Put it on a mat. Say why. Every fifth card, act out a bonus card!
flow.parent: Answers. Lungs: cow, Ganges river dolphin, crow, python, elephant, sea turtle, bar-headed goose, bat, human baby, whale. Gills: rohu fish, tadpole, crab, prawn, shark, goldfish. Skin: earthworm, lungless salamander. Two ways: frog (lungs and skin), mudskipper (gills and skin), climbing perch (gills and an air-breathing room). Air pipes: grasshopper, butterfly, ant.

check.q: Card: Ganges river dolphin. It lives in water all its life. Where does it go?
options: LUNGS
GILLS
SKIN
check.why: Dolphins breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole. They come up every minute or two. Picking 'gills' usually means thinking that everything living in water breathes water. Living in water is not the same as breathing water.

flow.context: This is the main part of Lungs, Gills or Skin? You take turns sorting animal cards.

flow.kid: Count your tokens. Which animal surprised you most? Why?

rules: Everyone stands in a circle holding hands. This is the cave wall.
One player is the bat and wears a blindfold. One is the moth. One or two are trees, who stand still inside the circle.
The bat calls 'Bat!'. The moth must answer 'Moth!' straight away. Trees answer 'Tree!' if the bat is within two steps of them.
The bat uses the echoes, the answers, to find and tag the moth without touching a tree.
Time each round. Swap roles. The fastest bat wins.
games.context: Bat and Moth is a running game, like the Indian blindfold game, that shows how bats find insects in the dark by echolocation.

flow.do: 1. Make the circle. 2. Hand out the role cards. 3. Tie the blindfold on the bat.
flow.say: Bats hunt moths at night. Many bats can see, but in the dark they mostly listen. They shout very high sounds and listen for the echo. Our bat will shout 'Bat!' and listen for 'Moth!'.
flow.kid: Make a circle. The bat wears a blindfold. The bat calls 'Bat!'. The moth must answer 'Moth!'.
flow.parent: Play on grass or a clear floor. The circle keeps the bat safe. Bats are not blind. Many see well, but they use sound in the dark.
flow.context: This is the first step of Bat and Moth. You set up a game that shows how bats hunt with echoes.

flow.do: Play rounds of about a minute each. Time each round. Swap roles so everyone is the bat once.
flow.say: Bat, call as often as you like. Moth, you must answer every time. Trees, warn the bat if it comes close.
flow.kid: Bat: call and listen. Moth: always answer. Trees: say 'Tree!' if the bat comes near.

check.q: In Bat and Moth, the blindfolded bat found the moth by listening. What does a real bat listen for?
options: Echoes of its own high sounds bouncing off insects
The flap of the moth's wings only
Nothing, it smells the moth
check.why: Real bats send out sounds too high for us to hear. The sounds bounce off insects and come back as echoes. That's echolocation. Picking 'wing flaps' is not silly: some bats do also listen for the sounds prey makes. But mostly they use their own echoes.

flow.context: This is the main part of Bat and Moth. You play rounds, taking turns as the bat.

flow.do: Talk about how it felt to find food by sound.
flow.say: How did it feel to be the bat? Did it get easier with practice? Ganges river dolphins hunt fish in muddy water the same way, with clicks.
flow.kid: Was it hard to be the bat? Did it get easier? River dolphins hunt like this in muddy water.
flow.think: Moths have ears too. What might a clever moth do when it hears a bat coming?
flow.context: This is the end of Bat and Moth. You talk about finding food by sound.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: the basics

items.p: Why does every animal need oxygen?
opts: Its cells use oxygen to get energy from food
Only so it can make sounds
It doesn't, only people need oxygen
items.why: Every cell uses oxygen to unlock the energy in food. This is respiration. Picking 'only people' is a common idea, but fish, worms, ants and elephants all need oxygen too.

items.p: Fish take oxygen out of water with their ____.
items.why: Gills are the feathery red parts under the flaps on a fish's head. Water flows over them and they take oxygen out.

items.p: An earthworm has no lungs. It breathes through its damp ____.
items.why: Oxygen passes straight through an earthworm's thin, moist skin. If the skin dries out, it cannot breathe.

items.p: A dolphin breathes with gills, like a fish.
items.why: False. Dolphins breathe air with lungs, through the blowhole on top of the head. That's why they keep coming up to the surface.

items.p: Breathed-out air still has some oxygen in it.
items.why: True. Room air is about 21 parts in 100 oxygen. Breathed-out air is about 16 parts in 100. Your body keeps only a little each breath.

items.p: Sort these animals by how they mainly breathe.
items.why: Land animals like cows and crows use lungs. So do dolphins, even though they live in water. Fish and crabs use gills. Earthworms and lungless salamanders breathe only through their skin.

items.p: Match each animal to how it mainly finds food.
items.why: Each animal relies most on the sense that suits its life. Bats hunt in the dark by echoes. Dogs follow smells. Eagles see far. Owls hear mice in the dark. Pit vipers feel the warmth of a mouse.

items.p: Look at the breath count chart. How many more breaths were taken after jumping than sitting still?
items.why: Sitting still the bar shows 20. After jumping it shows 40. 40 take away 20 is 20. Picking 40 means reading only one bar. To compare, we find the difference between the two bars.

chart.title: Made-up results: breaths in one minute

items.context: In the Breath Count experiment, you counted your breaths for one minute sitting still, then just after jumping.

items.p: In the chuna water test, which glass turned milky first?
opts: The one with room air from a pump
items.why: Carbon dioxide turns chuna water milky, and breathed-out air has much more carbon dioxide than room air. Picking 'both' would mean the two kinds of air were the same, but the test showed they are not.
items.context: In the Chuna Water Test, you bubbled your breath into one glass of chuna water and pumped room air into another.

items.p: Put the journey of oxygen in order, from outside to a cell in your leg.
items: tiny air sacs in the lungs
items.why: Air comes in through the nose, down the windpipe, into the tiny air sacs. Oxygen passes into the blood, and the blood carries it to every cell.

items.p: Why is a fish's gill made of many thin, frilly threads?
opts: To give lots of surface for oxygen to pass through
To keep sand out of its eyes
items.why: More surface lets more oxygen in at once. Remember the towel test: the frilly towel dried much faster than the crumpled one. Picking 'swim faster' mixes gills up with fins.
items.context: In the gill shape test, you hung up a crumpled wet towel and a frilly wet towel to see which dried first.

items.p: Draw a fish. Draw arrows to show where water goes in and where it goes out. Colour the gills.
items.a: An arrow into the mouth, an arrow out from under the gill cover, and red gills under the cover.
items.why: Water goes in at the mouth, flows over the gills, and goes out under the gill cover.
items.art: The outline of a fish side-on, with a dotted line where the gill cover is.

items.p: Animals breathe faster when they are resting.
items.why: False. Animals breathe faster when they are active, because their muscles need more oxygen. Resting and sleeping animals breathe slowest.

items.p: A flamingo sieves tiny shrimps from lake water. What kind of eater is it?
items.why: A filter feeder sieves tiny food out of water. A scavenger eats animals that have already died. A grazer eats grass or plants slowly for hours.

items.p: Why do frogs need to stay near water? Use the word skin in your answer.
items.a: Frogs breathe partly through their skin. Their skin must stay damp for oxygen to pass through. If they go too far from water, their skin dries out and they cannot breathe well.
items.why: Skin breathing only works when the skin is thin and damp.

items.p: Ants on a sugar trail walk in a line. Why?
opts: They follow a smell trail left by the first ant
The wind blows them in a line
items.why: The ant that finds food leaves a smell trail on its way home. Other ants follow it with their antennae. That's why they walk in a line.
items.context: In Ant Detectives, you put out sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path and watched the ants come.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: think further

items.p: A fish has gills full of blood. Out of water, it usually dies, even though air has more oxygen than water. Why?
opts: Its soft gill threads stick together and dry out, so there is too little surface
items.why: Out of water, the thin gill threads collapse and stick together, like a wet paintbrush pulled out of a jar. Then there is too little damp surface for oxygen to pass through. Picking 'poisonous' is a common idea, but air is not poisonous. Some fish, like the climbing perch, can even breathe it.

items.p: Your diaphragm is a sheet of muscle under your lungs. What does it do when you breathe in?
opts: It pulls down, making space, and air rushes into the lungs
It pushes air up into the nose
items.why: When the diaphragm pulls down, there is more space in the chest, and air flows in to fill it. That's what the bottle lung showed. Picking 'pushes air up' is what happens when you breathe out, not in.
items.context: In Make a Bottle Lung, you pulled the stretchy balloon at the bottom of a bottle and watched the balloon inside fill.

items.p: Insects have small lungs inside their bodies.
items.why: False. Insects have no lungs. Air goes in through tiny holes called spiracles along their sides, and travels down thin pipes to every part of the body.

items.p: The tiny holes along the sides of a grasshopper, where air goes in, are called ____.
items.why: Spiracles lead into air pipes that branch through the insect's body.

items.p: The climbing perch can live out of water for hours. What lets it do this?
opts: An extra breathing room above its gills that takes oxygen from air
It holds its breath for a very long time
It doesn't need oxygen when it's dry
items.why: The climbing perch has a maze-like breathing room above its gills. It can gulp air and take oxygen from it, as long as its body stays damp. Picking 'holds its breath' would only work for a short time.

items.p: Match each way of getting food to an animal that uses it.
items.why: Each animal's body fits its way of eating: flat teeth for grazing, long legs for chasing, stillness for waiting, a sieve beak for filtering, a web for trapping, and a strong stomach for scavenging.

items.p: Look at the ant chart. How many ants were on the sugar and biscuit together?
items.why: 24 ants on the sugar plus 15 on the biscuit makes 24 + 15 = 39. Picking 25 means adding the sugar and the salt instead. Read the labels under each bar carefully.

chart.title: Made-up results: ants on each bait after 30 minutes

items.context: In Ant Detectives, you counted ants on three baits after 30 minutes.

items.p: A Ganges river dolphin is nearly blind and lives in muddy water. How does it find fish?
opts: It sends out clicks and listens to the echoes
It sees them with big eyes
It waits for fish to jump into its mouth
items.why: The Ganges river dolphin uses echolocation. It sends out clicks, and the echoes tell it where fish are. Its eyes are tiny because seeing doesn't help much in muddy water.

items.p: A mosquito can find you in the dark by sensing the carbon dioxide you breathe out.
items.why: True. Mosquitoes sense carbon dioxide from a distance, then follow warmth and smell close up.

items.p: Put these in order, from fewest breaths a minute to most: elephant, child, mouse.
items.why: Big animals usually breathe more slowly than small ones. An elephant takes only a few breaths a minute. A child takes about 20. A mouse takes more than 100.

items.p: In the chuna water test, why did we also pump room air into a second glass?
items.a: To make it a fair test. We needed to compare breathed-out air with ordinary air. If only the breath glass went milky, we know it was something in the breath, carbon dioxide, and not just bubbles.
items.why: A comparison shows that the milkiness comes from what is in breath, not from bubbling.
items.context: In the Chuna Water Test, one glass got breathed-out air and the other got room air from a pump.

items.p: Why do mammals like dolphins and whales store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles?
opts: So they can stay underwater longer while hunting
items.why: Diving animals can't breathe underwater. Extra stored oxygen lets them hunt for longer before coming up. Some deep-diving whales stay down for over an hour.

items.p: Label the parts on the drawing of the breathing system: nose, windpipe, lungs, diaphragm.
items.why: Air goes in through the nose, down the windpipe, into the lungs. The diaphragm under the lungs pulls down to bring air in.
items.art: An outline of a child's upper body with the breathing system drawn in and four blank label lines.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out, and why? Earthworm, rohu fish, crab, prawn.
items.why: The earthworm breathes through its skin. The rohu, crab and prawn all breathe with gills.

items.p: A cheetah hunts by chasing. A crocodile hunts by waiting. Which do you think needs to breathe faster while hunting? Why?
items.a: The cheetah. Chasing at high speed uses a lot of muscle, and working muscles need a lot of oxygen. A crocodile waiting still uses very little oxygen.
items.why: Breathing rate goes with how hard the muscles are working.

worksheets.title: Breathing and finding food: big thinking

items.p: Lungs, gills and frog skin look very different. Write three things they all have in common.
items.a: They are thin. They are damp. They have lots of surface, and blood flows just underneath.
items.why: All breathing surfaces work the same way: oxygen passes through a thin, wet wall into blood.

items.p: Water holds about 30 times less oxygen than air. What would you expect a fish to do in warm, still water with even less oxygen?
opts: Move its gill covers faster, or come to the surface
Sleep until the water gets better
items.why: With less oxygen in the water, a fish must push more water over its gills, so it pumps faster. Some fish come to the surface, where the water has a little more oxygen. Picking 'stop breathing' would be fatal. Every cell needs a steady supply.

items.p: The oxygen you breathe was put into the air by plants and tiny sea algae.
items.why: True. Plants and algae make oxygen when they make food from sunlight. Scientists think about half of the oxygen made each year comes from tiny algae in the sea.

items.p: Charles Darwin thought swim bladders came first and later turned into lungs. Many biologists today think the opposite. What does this show about science?
opts: Scientists change their ideas when new evidence comes in
items.why: Science improves when new evidence is found, such as studies of old kinds of fish and fossils. Darwin got many big things right. Changing one idea does not make all his work wrong.

items.p: Why can't you see oxygen going into your blood, even though it happens with every breath?
items.a: Oxygen is a gas with no colour. It passes into the blood through walls thinner than tissue paper, inside the lungs, where we can't see.
items.why: Some of the most important things in the body happen far too small to see.

items.p: Some bats eat moths. Many moths can hear bat sounds. What might a moth do when it hears a bat?
opts: Dive, dodge or drop to the ground
items.why: Many moths dodge or drop when they hear a bat's high sounds. Some even make clicks that confuse bats. Predator and prey keep changing each other over a very long time.

items.p: Earthworms come up onto roads after rain. Scientists have three ideas: to breathe, to travel, or to escape moles. Pick the one you think is most likely and say how you could test it.
items.a: For example: I think they come up to travel. I could put worms in two trays of soil, one wet and one dry, and see where they move. Or I could put a worm in a jar of water that has air bubbled through it, and see if it stays healthy.
items.why: Any careful test idea is a good answer. Scientists are still testing these ideas.

items.p: A Cuvier's beaked whale stayed underwater for 222 minutes. About how many hours is that?
items.why: One hour is 60 minutes. Four hours is 240 minutes. 222 is a bit less than 240, so nearly 4 hours. Picking 22 hours means reading the digits instead of dividing by 60.

items.p: Every cell in your body uses oxygen, not just your lungs.
items.why: True. The lungs only bring oxygen in. Every cell, in your toes, your brain and your eyes, uses it to get energy from food.

items.p: The tiny energy parts in your cells, called mitochondria, use oxygen. Where did scientists find out they came from?
opts: Tiny bacteria that moved into bigger cells long ago
items.why: Lynn Margulis argued in 1967 that mitochondria came from bacteria living inside bigger cells. DNA tests later showed she was right. So every breath you take feeds tiny partners that were once bacteria.

items.p: Kamala Sohonie was the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, in 1939. She found that plant cells have cytochrome c, a substance animal cells also use in breathing. What does her discovery tell us about plants and animals?
items.a: Plants and animals use some of the same parts to breathe. Their cells work in a similar way, even though they look so different.
items.why: Under the skin and the bark, life shares the same tools.

items.p: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas, where the air is thin. What does 'thin air' mean for breathing?
opts: Each breath has less oxygen in it
The air is very cold, so it can't be breathed
There is no air at all
items.why: High up, the air is spread out more, so each breath carries less oxygen. Bar-headed geese have lungs, blood and hearts that grab oxygen extra well. Picking 'no air at all' is too strong. There is air, just less of it in each breath.

items.p: Sort these senses: which ones do people have, and which do only some other animals have?
items.why: People see, hear, smell, taste and touch. Bats and dolphins use echolocation. Pit vipers sense heat. Sharks feel electricity. Some blind people do learn to use clicks and echoes too, which shows how much a brain can learn.

items.p: Design a breathing part for an animal that lives in thick mud with almost no oxygen. Draw it and explain why it would work.
items.a: For example: a long tube like a snorkel reaching up to the air, or skin with many folds to give lots of surface, or a mouth that gulps air like the climbing perch.
items.why: Good designs give lots of surface, stay damp, or reach air.

items.p: A gill takes oxygen from water. A lung takes oxygen from air. A frog's skin takes oxygen from both. What do all three really do?
opts: Let oxygen pass through a thin, damp wall into blood
items.why: All three are thin, damp walls with blood underneath. Oxygen passes through into the blood. Picking 'make oxygen' mixes animals up with plants. Plants and algae make oxygen. Animals only take it in.

experiments.title: Breath Count: before and after jumping
experiments.question: Do we breathe faster after exercise? How much faster?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. How many breaths do you take in one minute while sitting still? Will the number go up, go down or stay the same after one minute of jumping?
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, count in the same way every time: sit in the same chair, and count for the same time. Only one thing changes: resting or just after jumping. Count 3 times for each, because one count can be a fluke.

materials.item: a clock, phone or sand timer that shows one minute
a pencil and the results table
a grown-up or friend to count with you

experiments.safety: Jump on a flat, non-slippery floor, away from furniture. Stop if you feel dizzy or unwell. Children with asthma can skip the jumping and count a grown-up's breaths instead.

schedule.what: Guess. Count breaths sitting still, 3 times. Jump for one minute. Count again. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw two bars: one for resting, one for after jumping. Then write a claim, your evidence and your reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment you count your breaths in one minute, sitting still and then just after jumping, to see if exercise changes breathing.
