setup.caption: 2. Jump on the spot for one minute.

setup.art: The child sitting again, panting, hand on chest, while the grown-up writes a number in a table.
setup.caption: 3. Sit down straight away. Count your breaths for one minute again.

flow.do: 1. Sit your child on a chair. 2. Ask them to guess how many breaths they take in one minute. 3. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Each time your chest goes up and down, that is one breath. How many breaths do you think you take in one minute, sitting still? And after jumping, will it be more or fewer?
flow.kid: One breath is one up and one down of your chest. How many breaths in a minute? Guess a number. Write it down.

ask.q: What do you think will happen after jumping? Why?
good: More breaths, because I will be puffed out.
Faster, because my body needs more air when I move.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Breath Count experiment. You guess how many breaths you take in one minute.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still for one minute first, to settle. 2. They put one hand flat on their chest. 3. Start the timer. They count each rise of the chest, quietly. 4. Stop at one minute and write the number. 5. Rest one minute and repeat, until there are 3 counts.
flow.say: Put your hand on your chest. Breathe normally, don't try to change it. I'll say go, and you count each time your chest rises. Ready? Go.
flow.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your chest. Breathe normally. Count each time your chest goes up. Stop when the minute ends. Write the number. Do it three times.
flow.parent: Most children of 6 to 10 take about 18 to 25 breaths a minute at rest. It's fine if the first count is odd, because counting your own breath changes it a little. That's why we count three times. If counting is hard, the grown-up can watch and count instead.

chart.title: Made-up example: how to fill in the table

flow.context: This is the step where you count your breaths while sitting still, three times.

flow.do: 1. Your child jumps on the spot for one full minute. 2. The moment the minute ends, they sit down. 3. Start the timer straight away and count breaths for one minute. 4. Write the number. 5. Rest three minutes, then repeat twice more.
flow.say: Now jump on the spot for one whole minute, as fast as is comfortable. The second I say stop, sit down, hand on chest, and we count straight away.
flow.kid: Jump on the spot for one minute. Then sit down fast. Hand on your chest. Count your breaths for one minute. Write the number.
flow.parent: Watch for dizziness and let your child stop early if needed. Count straight away, because breathing slows back down within a few minutes. Wait until breathing feels normal before the next jump.
flow.context: This is the step where you jump for one minute and then count your breaths again.

flow.do: 1. Find the middle value of each set of three counts: put them in order and take the middle one. 2. Draw two bars, one for sitting still and one for after jumping.
flow.say: Let's turn our numbers into a picture. One bar for resting. One bar for after jumping. The taller the bar, the more breaths in a minute.
flow.kid: Put your three numbers in order. The middle one is your middle value. Draw a bar for resting. Draw a bar for after jumping.

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Yours will be different.

check.q: In the breath count chart, the bar for after jumping is taller. What does that tell us?
options: We breathe more times in a minute after jumping
We breathe fewer times after jumping
Jumping makes us taller
check.why: Each bar shows how many breaths were counted in one minute. A taller bar means more breaths. Picking 'fewer' usually means the bars were read the wrong way round. Look at the numbers on the side of the chart to check.

flow.context: This is the step where you turn your breath counts into a bar chart.

flow.do: Help your child say or write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's explain what we found, like a scientist. First, what do you think? That's your claim. Then, what did you see? That's your evidence. Then, why? That's your reasoning.
flow.kid: Say what you found. Then say what numbers showed it. Then say why it happened.

ask.q: Claim: what happens to breathing after exercise?
good: We breathe faster after exercise.

ask.q: Evidence: what did your numbers show?
good: Sitting still I took 20 breaths a minute. After jumping I took 40.

ask.q: Reasoning: why?
good: My leg muscles were working hard. They needed more oxygen, so I breathed faster to get more air in.
My muscles made more carbon dioxide, and I had to breathe it out.

check.q: Why do we breathe faster after jumping?
options: Our muscles need more oxygen to get energy from food
Our lungs get tired and slow down
Jumping shakes extra air into our nose
check.why: Working muscles do more respiration, which means they use more oxygen to unlock energy from food. Breathing faster brings that oxygen in and takes the extra carbon dioxide out. Picking 'lungs get tired' mixes up breathing with tiredness. Picking 'shakes air in' means thinking air gets in by itself, but our muscles pull it in.

flow.think: A cheetah after a chase pants very hard. A sleeping python breathes only a few times a minute. Why might that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Breath Count experiment. You explain what you found, using claim, evidence and reasoning.

experiments.title: The Chuna Water Test: what is in your breath?
experiments.question: Is the air we breathe out different from the air in the room?
experiments.predict: Guess first. If we bubble breathed-out air into chuna water, and pump room air into another glass of chuna water, will they look the same at the end?
experiments.fair_test: Both glasses get the same amount of chuna water, the same straw, and air bubbled in for the same time. Only the kind of air changes: breathed-out air or room air from a bicycle pump.

materials.item: edible chuna, the white lime paste sold at paan shops
a bicycle pump or a balloon pump

experiments.safety: Chuna is strong and can sting skin and eyes. Only a grown-up mixes it. Never drink chuna water. Blow OUT through the straw only, never suck. Wash hands afterwards. Pour the water down the sink with plenty of water.

schedule.what: A grown-up stirs one teaspoon of chuna into a jug of water and leaves it overnight to settle.
Pour off the clear chuna water. Bubble breath into one glass and pump room air into the other. Compare.

experiments.record: Draw the two glasses after 2 minutes. Write which one turned milky first. Then write your claim, evidence and reasoning.
experiments.context: In this experiment you use clear chuna water, which turns milky when carbon dioxide bubbles through it, to find out whether breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide than room air.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring a spoon of white chuna paste into a steel jug of water, then the jug resting overnight with white powder settled at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up mixes chuna in water. Leave it overnight.

setup.art: Two clear glasses of clear chuna water side by side: a child blowing gently through a straw into one, a bicycle pump pushing air through a straw into the other.
setup.caption: 2. Blow breath into one glass. Pump room air into the other.

setup.art: The same two glasses after two minutes: the breath glass cloudy white like milk, the pump glass still almost clear.
setup.caption: 3. Compare. Which one turned milky?

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Stir one level teaspoon of edible chuna into a jug of tap water. 2. Leave it covered overnight, away from children.
flow.say: This is chuna, the lime paste people put on paan leaves. Mixed with water, it makes a special water that changes when carbon dioxide gets into it. It's strong, so only I touch it.
flow.kid: Today a grown-up mixes chuna in water. Chuna stings, so don't touch it. Tomorrow you will use the clear water.
flow.wait: Leave the jug overnight so the white powder settles.
flow.parent: Edible chuna is calcium hydroxide. Mixed with water and settled, the clear liquid on top is limewater, used in school labs. Keep it out of reach overnight.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Chuna Water Test. A grown-up makes limewater from chuna, the lime paste sold at paan shops.

flow.do: Day 2. 1. Gently pour the clear water from the top of the jug into two glasses, half full each. Leave the white powder behind. 2. Put a straw in each glass.
flow.say: Look, both glasses are clear. Carbon dioxide turns this water milky. Which kind of air do you think has more carbon dioxide: your breath, or the air in this room?
flow.kid: Look at the two glasses. Both are clear. Guess. Which will turn milky: your breath or room air?

ask.q: Which glass do you think will turn milky first? Why?
good: The breath one, because we breathe out carbon dioxide.
The breath one, because our body puts used air out.

flow.context: This is the step where you pour the clear chuna water into two glasses and make a guess.

flow.do: 1. Your child blows gently OUT through the straw in glass 1, for one minute, taking breaths in through the nose. 2. A grown-up pushes the bicycle pump slowly through the straw in glass 2 for the same minute. 3. Check both glasses at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 2 minutes.
flow.say: Blow out gently through the straw, slow bubbles. Breathe in through your nose, never through the straw. I'll pump room air into the other glass at the same time.
flow.kid: Breathe in through your nose. Blow out gently through the straw. Never suck. Watch the bubbles. A grown-up pumps air in the other glass.
flow.parent: The breath glass usually goes cloudy within 30 seconds to a minute. The pump glass stays nearly clear for many minutes, because room air has only a tiny bit of carbon dioxide. If your child sucks by mistake, rinse their mouth with plenty of water.
flow.context: This is the step where you bubble your breath into one glass of chuna water, and room air into the other.

flow.do: Compare the glasses and talk about claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you see? The milky colour is chalk, tiny bits of it, made when carbon dioxide meets the chuna. So which air had more carbon dioxide?
flow.kid: Which glass turned milky? Milky means carbon dioxide. What does that tell you about your breath?

ask.q: Claim: is breathed-out air different from room air?
good: Yes. Breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide.

ask.q: Evidence?
good: The breath glass went milky in under a minute. The pump glass stayed clear.

ask.q: Reasoning?
good: My cells use oxygen and make carbon dioxide. My blood carries it to my lungs, and I breathe it out.

check.q: The chuna water with breath turned milky. The one with room air stayed clear. Why?
options: Breathed-out air has much more carbon dioxide than room air
Breathed-out air has no oxygen at all
Spit from the straw made it milky
check.why: Carbon dioxide turns chuna water milky, and breathed-out air carries carbon dioxide made by your cells. Picking 'no oxygen at all' is a common mistake. Breathed-out air still has a lot of oxygen, just a bit less. Picking 'spit' is a good scientist's worry. To check, add a few drops of water from a clean straw to the room-air glass. It stays clear.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Chuna Water Test. You compare the two glasses and explain what happened.

experiments.title: Ant Detectives: which food do ants find first?
experiments.question: How do ants find food? Do they find some foods faster than others?
experiments.predict: Guess first. We will put out three baits: sugar, salt and a crumb of biscuit. Which will the first ant find? Which will have the most ants after 30 minutes?
experiments.fair_test: Put the three baits the same size, the same distance from the ants' path, on the same kind of paper, at the same time. Only the food changes. Count the ants on each bait at 10, 20 and 30 minutes.

materials.item: three small squares of white paper or card
a pinch of sugar, a pinch of salt, a crumb of biscuit
a timer and the results table

experiments.safety: Use common small black ants, not red fire ants or big biting ants. Watch, don't touch. Clean up the baits afterwards so ants don't come into the kitchen.

schedule.what: Find an ant path. Lay out three baits. Count ants every 10 minutes for 30 minutes. Watch how they find the food.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw a bar chart of ants at 30 minutes. Draw a map of the ant trail you saw.
experiments.context: In this experiment you put out sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path, and count how many ants find each one. It shows how ants use smell to find food.

setup.art: Three small white paper squares on a garden path, one with sugar, one with salt, one with a biscuit crumb, each the same distance from a line of small black ants.
setup.caption: 1. Put three baits the same distance from an ant path.

setup.art: A child with a magnifying glass crouched over the sugar square, with ants gathering on it and a timer beside.
setup.caption: 2. Count the ants on each bait every 10 minutes.

setup.art: A line of ants walking in single file from the sugar back to a crack in the wall, following an invisible dotted smell trail.
setup.caption: 3. Watch how the ants follow each other back home.

flow.do: 1. Go outside, or to a corner where ants already walk. 2. Find a line of small black ants. 3. Put the three paper squares about one hand-length from the line, side by side, a hand-length apart. 4. Put the sugar, salt and biscuit crumb on them.
flow.say: Ants have no noses, but they smell with their feelers, the two thin antennae on their heads. Let's see if they can find our food. Which one do you think they'll find first?
flow.kid: Find a line of ants. Put three papers near it. Put sugar on one, salt on one, biscuit on one. Which will ants find first?

ask.q: How do you think an ant knows where food is?
good: It smells it.
It feels it with its feelers.
Other ants show it the way.

flow.context: This is the first step of Ant Detectives. You put three kinds of food near an ant path.

flow.do: 1. Start the timer. 2. Watch quietly. Note which bait the first ant reaches, and how long it took. 3. At 10, 20 and 30 minutes, count the ants on each bait and write the numbers in the table. 4. In between, watch one ant leave the food and follow it.
flow.say: Look, one ant found the sugar. Watch what it does next. Does it go home? Does it touch other ants? Let's count every ten minutes.
flow.kid: Watch quietly. Which food did the first ant find? Count the ants on each paper every ten minutes. Follow one ant with your eyes.
flow.parent: Usually one scout ant finds the sugar or biscuit by smell, wanders back towards the nest, and soon a trail of ants arrives. The scout leaves a smell trail, called a pheromone trail, on the way home. Salt usually gets few or no ants. Results vary with the kind of ant, so whatever happens is real data.

chart.title: Made-up example: ants on each bait after 30 minutes
chart.note: Made-up numbers to show what a chart can look like. Your ants will be different.

flow.context: This is the step where you watch and count the ants on each bait for 30 minutes.

flow.do: Talk about what you saw, using claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: So, what do we think? How do ants find food? What did you see that tells you? And why do the other ants arrive in a line?
flow.kid: Say what you found. What numbers show it? Why did the ants walk in a line?

ask.q: Claim?
good: Ants find sweet food by smell, and they find sugar faster than salt.

ask.q: Evidence?
good: After 30 minutes there were 24 ants on the sugar and only 1 on the salt.
The ants walked in a line from the sugar to their nest.

ask.q: Reasoning?
good: Sugar is energy food. The first ant smelled it and left a smell trail home. The others followed the trail.

check.q: Ants arrived at the sugar in a long line. How did they know the way?
options: They followed a smell trail left by the first ant
They could see the sugar from far away
They heard the sugar
check.why: Ants that find food leave a trail of smell on the way back to the nest. Other ants follow it with their antennae. Most small ants see poorly, so picking 'see' is a good guess but not how they do it. Try this: rub a finger across the trail. Watch the ants get confused where the smell is wiped away.

flow.think: If you wipe your finger across the ant trail, what will the ants do? Try it gently and see.
flow.context: This is the last step of Ant Detectives. You explain how the ants found the food.

activities.title: Breath on a Steel Tumbler

materials.item: a steel tumbler or steel plate, cooled in the fridge for 10 minutes

activities.safety: Nothing to worry about. Just don't put the cold tumbler on your eyes.
activities.record: Draw what you saw on the tumbler and the tissue. Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.
activities.context: This is a short noticing activity to start the unit. You breathe on cold steel, a mirror and a tissue, and notice what your breath does.

setup.art: A child breathing out slowly onto a shiny cold steel tumbler, a misty patch forming on it.
setup.caption: 1. Breathe out slowly onto a cold steel tumbler.

setup.art: The child holding a thin strip of tissue under the nose, the tissue fluttering outwards.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a tissue strip under your nose. Watch it move.

setup.art: The child with one hand on the chest and one on the belly, both rising, eyes closed.
setup.caption: 3. Put a hand on your chest and one on your belly. Feel them move.

flow.do: 1. Take the steel tumbler out of the fridge. 2. Your child breathes out slowly onto it, three times. 3. Then onto the mirror. 4. Then holds a tissue strip under their nose and breathes in and out.
flow.say: Breathe out slowly onto the cold steel. What appears? Now hold the tissue under your nose. What does it do when you breathe in? When you breathe out?
flow.kid: Breathe out on the cold steel. What do you see? Hold the tissue under your nose. Watch it move.

ask.q: What do you notice?
good: The steel goes misty.
Little drops of water appear.
The tissue blows away when I breathe out and comes closer when I breathe in.

ask.q: What do you wonder?
good: Where does the water come from?
Does a fish breathe like this?
What is in my breath?

flow.parent: The mist is water. Breath is warm and damp, and the water in it turns into tiny drops on cold steel. Don't explain more yet. The unit will answer the child's wonders.
flow.context: This is the first step of Breath on a Steel Tumbler. You breathe on cold steel and a tissue and notice what happens.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits still, one hand on the chest and one on the belly. 2. They breathe normally for ten breaths and notice which hand moves. 3. Then they take three big slow breaths.
flow.say: Close your eyes. One hand on your chest, one on your belly. Just notice. Which hand moves? Now take a big slow breath in. Where does the air go?
flow.kid: Close your eyes. One hand on your chest. One hand on your belly. Breathe. Which hand moves? Now take a big, slow breath.

check.q: Your breath made the cold steel tumbler misty. What is the mist?
options: Tiny drops of water from your breath
Smoke from inside your body
Oxygen you can see
check.why: Your breath is warm and damp. When it touches cold steel, the water in it turns into tiny drops, just like drops on a cold glass of water. Picking 'smoke' means thinking breathing is like burning, which is partly a good idea, but there is no smoke. Oxygen has no colour, so you can never see it.

flow.think: You breathed out water. Where did that water come from? A fish lives in water. How does it breathe?
flow.context: This is the step where you feel your chest and belly move as you breathe.

activities.title: Make a Bottle Lung

materials.item: a clear plastic bottle, about 1 litre
scissors or a cutter, for a grown-up

activities.safety: Only a grown-up cuts the bottle. Cover the cut edge with tape so it isn't sharp.
activities.record: Draw your bottle lung. Label the balloon lung, the windpipe and the diaphragm. Draw arrows showing which way air goes when you pull down.
activities.context: In this activity you build a model lung from a bottle and two balloons, to see how a sheet of muscle under the lungs pulls air in.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting the bottom off a clear plastic bottle, tape ready on the table.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom off a bottle.

setup.art: A balloon hanging inside the bottle from its neck, and a second balloon, knotted and cut, stretched over the open bottom like a drum.
setup.caption: 2. Hang one balloon inside. Stretch the other over the bottom.

setup.art: A child pulling the knot of the bottom balloon down, the balloon inside the bottle puffing up with air.
setup.caption: 3. Pull the bottom balloon down. Watch the lung fill.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts off the bottom third of the bottle and tapes the edge. 2. Push one balloon into the bottle neck, stretching its mouth over the outside of the neck. 3. Tie a knot in the second balloon, cut off its top half, and stretch the rest over the open bottom of the bottle. 4. Tape it so it is airtight.
flow.say: We're going to build a lung. The balloon inside is the lung. The bottle neck is the windpipe. The stretchy balloon at the bottom is the diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Put one balloon inside the neck. Stretch the other over the bottom. That one is your diaphragm.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make a Bottle Lung. You build a model lung from a bottle and two balloons.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the bottle with one hand. 2. With the other, they pull the knot of the bottom balloon gently down. 3. Watch the inside balloon. 4. Then let go.
flow.say: Pull the bottom balloon down, slowly. What happens to the lung? Now let go. What happens? This is what your diaphragm does every time you breathe.
flow.kid: Pull the bottom balloon down. What does the inside balloon do? Let go. What happens now?

ask.q: What happened when you pulled down?
good: The inside balloon filled up with air.
The lung got bigger.

ask.q: Why do you think it filled up?
good: Pulling down made more space inside the bottle, and air rushed in through the neck to fill the balloon.

check.q: In the bottle lung, you pulled the bottom balloon down and the inside balloon filled. What does the bottom balloon stand for?
options: The diaphragm, the muscle under the lungs
The nose
The heart
check.why: The bottom balloon is the diaphragm. In your body, it pulls down to make space, and air rushes into your lungs. Picking 'the nose' usually means thinking we suck air in with our nose. The nose is just the door. The pulling is done by the diaphragm.

flow.context: This is the step where you pull the bottom balloon and watch the model lung fill with air.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts a hand on their belly and breathes in deeply. 2. Compare it with the bottle lung. 3. Talk about what the model gets right and what it gets wrong.
flow.say: Every model is a little wrong. Real lungs aren't one balloon. They're like a sponge with 480 million tiny bubbles. What else is different in your body?
flow.kid: Breathe in deeply. Feel your belly push out. That's your diaphragm pulling down. How is the bottle different from your real lungs?

ask.q: How is the model different from real lungs?
good: We have two lungs, not one.
Real lungs are spongy, with millions of tiny bubbles.
Our ribs move too.
There is blood all around real lungs.

flow.parent: Children love finding what's wrong with a model. It's real science thinking: a model shows one idea, not everything.
flow.think: A fish has no diaphragm. How does it move water over its gills?
flow.context: This is the step where you compare the bottle lung with your own breathing, and find what the model gets wrong.

activities.title: Gill Watch: count a fish's breaths

materials.item: a fish to watch: a home aquarium, a pet shop tank, a temple tank or pond, or a fish at the market

activities.safety: Stay with a grown-up near ponds and tanks. Do not tap on aquarium glass. At a fish market, only look, and wash hands if you touch anything.

schedule.what: Gill Watch: count a fish's breaths

activities.record: Write how many times the fish's gill covers opened in one minute. Draw the fish and colour its gills.
activities.context: In this activity you watch a live fish and count how many times its gill covers open in one minute. If you can, you also look at the red gills of a fish at the market.

setup.art: A child kneeling in front of a home fish tank, watching a goldfish whose gill flaps are opening, a timer in hand.
setup.caption: 1. Watch the flaps behind a fish's eyes open and shut.

setup.art: A child making a tally mark in a notebook for each flap.
setup.caption: 2. Count each opening for one minute.

setup.art: A fish seller at an Indian market lifting the gill cover of a fresh fish to show bright red gills.
setup.caption: 3. At the market, look at the red gills under the flap.

flow.do: 1. Find one fish that is calm. 2. Look just behind its eyes at the gill covers, the flaps on each side. 3. Watch its mouth open and shut. 4. Count each time the gill covers open, for one minute, making a tally mark each time.
flow.say: See the flaps behind its eyes? That's where the water goes out. It comes in at the mouth and goes out there, over the gills. Let's count how many times they open in one minute.
flow.kid: Look behind the fish's eyes. See the flaps? They open and shut. Count each opening for one minute. Make a tally mark each time.
flow.parent: Small fish in warm water often open their gill covers 60 to 100 times a minute, much faster than we breathe. Counting is hard, so 30 seconds doubled is fine.
flow.context: This is the first step of Gill Watch. You count how many times a fish's gill covers open in one minute.

flow.do: If you can, visit a fish market or ask at the fish counter. Ask the seller to lift the gill cover of a fresh fish. Look at the colour and shape of the gills.
flow.say: Fish sellers lift the gill flap to show how fresh a fish is. Bright red gills mean fresh. Why do you think they're so red?
flow.kid: Look under the flap of a fresh fish. See the red gills? They look like a comb with many thin teeth.

ask.q: Why are gills so red?
good: They are full of blood.
Blood comes close to the water there to pick up oxygen.

ask.q: Why do they have so many thin parts?
good: To have lots of surface, so they can catch more oxygen.

flow.context: This is the step where you look at the red gills of a fresh fish at the market.

flow.do: Compare the fish's count with your own breath count from the Breath Count experiment, if you did it.
flow.say: You took about 20 breaths a minute sitting still. The fish moved water over its gills many more times. Why might a fish have to work harder?
flow.kid: Was the fish's number bigger or smaller than yours? Why might a fish breathe so fast?

check.q: A small fish opened its gill covers 80 times a minute. You took 20 breaths. Why might the fish need so many?
options: Water has much less oxygen than air, so the fish moves lots of water
Fish are always frightened
Fish do not need oxygen, they just like moving water
check.why: Water holds far less oxygen than air, about thirty times less in the same space. So a fish must push a lot of water over its gills to get enough. Picking 'frightened' is a fair guess for a fish that's being watched, which is why we watch quietly. Picking 'fish don't need oxygen' is a common idea, but every animal needs oxygen.

flow.context: This is the last step of Gill Watch. You compare a fish's breathing with your own.

activities.title: Flat or Frilly? The gill shape test

materials.item: two paper towels or two pieces of tissue the same size
two clothes pegs and a string to hang them

activities.safety: Use child-safe scissors. Wipe up any spilled water.

schedule.what: Flat or Frilly? The gill shape test

activities.record: Write which towel dried first and how long each took. Draw both and label which is like a gill.
activities.context: In this activity you test why gills and lungs are frilly and folded. You wet two paper towels and see whether a crumpled one or a frilly cut one dries faster.

setup.art: Two identical paper towels, one crumpled into a tight ball, one cut into many thin frilly strips still joined at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Crumple one towel into a ball. Cut the other into frilly strips.

setup.art: Both towels being dipped in a bowl of water, then hung side by side with clothes pegs on a string.
setup.caption: 2. Wet both. Hang them side by side.

setup.art: A child touching the frilly towel, which is dry, while the crumpled ball is still dark and wet, a timer showing 40 minutes.
setup.caption: 3. Check every 10 minutes. Which one dries first?

flow.do: 1. Take two paper towels the same size. 2. Crumple one tightly into a ball. 3. Cut the other into thin strips, like a comb, leaving the top edge joined. 4. Dip both in water for 5 seconds, and squeeze each gently once. 5. Hang them side by side.
flow.say: Water leaves a wet towel through its surface, the outside that touches the air. Gills and lungs take oxygen in through their surface too. Which towel do you think has more surface touching the air?
flow.kid: Crumple one towel into a ball. Cut the other into thin strips. Wet both. Hang them up. Which one has more outside touching the air?

ask.q: Which towel will dry first? Why?
good: The frilly one, because more of it touches the air.
The frilly one, because the ball is all squashed inside.

flow.context: This is the first step of the gill shape test. You make one crumpled towel and one frilly towel and hang them up wet.

flow.do: Every 10 minutes, gently touch both towels and note how wet they feel: wet, damp or dry. Stop when one is dry.
flow.say: Let's check. Touch them gently. Which feels drier? The water is leaving through the surface, just as oxygen enters through the surface of a gill.
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, touch both towels. Wet, damp or dry? Write it down.
flow.parent: The frilly towel usually dries much faster, often in half the time or less. Same paper, same water. Only the shape changed. That's why it's a fair test.
flow.context: This is the step where you check the two towels every 10 minutes to see which dries first.

flow.do: Talk about what the result means for gills and lungs.
flow.say: Same paper, same water, but the frilly one let the water out much faster. Gills are frilly. Lungs have millions of tiny bubbles. What's the trick?
flow.kid: The frilly one dried faster. Gills are frilly too. Lungs have millions of tiny bubbles. Why?

check.q: In the towel test, the frilly towel dried faster than the crumpled ball. What does this tell us about gills?
options: Gills are frilly so that lots of surface can take in oxygen fast
Gills are frilly to look pretty
Gills are frilly because fish are always wet
check.why: More surface means more can pass through at once. Water left the frilly towel faster, and oxygen gets into frilly gills faster. Picking 'look pretty' is a fun answer, but body parts usually have shapes that help them work. Picking 'always wet' is half right. Gills do need to stay wet, but the frills are about surface.

flow.think: Out of water, a fish's gill threads stick together, like the crumpled towel. What happens to their surface then?
flow.context: This is the last step of the gill shape test. You work out why gills and lungs are frilly.

activities.title: Follow Your Nose: find the snack by smell

materials.item: five small steel bowls or cups, with paper covers that have small holes poked in them
a smelly snack, like a piece of banana, an elaichi pod or a little vanilla on cotton

activities.safety: Walk slowly when blindfolded, on a clear floor. A grown-up guides.

schedule.what: Follow Your Nose: find the snack by smell

activities.record: Write how many tries it took to find the snack by smell. Write which animal you would like to have the nose of, and why.
activities.context: In this activity you try to find a hidden snack only by smell, the way a dog or an ant does. Then you compare your nose with animal noses.

setup.art: Five covered steel bowls in a row on a floor, one hiding a piece of banana, paper covers with small holes.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up hides a smelly snack in one of five covered bowls.

setup.art: A blindfolded child on hands and knees, sniffing each bowl in turn like a dog.
setup.caption: 2. Wear a blindfold. Sniff each bowl.

setup.art: The child lifting the blindfold and pointing at the right bowl, smiling.
setup.caption: 3. Point to the bowl you think has the snack.

flow.do: 1. While your child is out of the room, put the snack in one bowl and cover all five. 2. Blindfold your child. 3. They sniff each bowl and choose one. 4. Try 3 rounds with different snacks.
flow.say: You're going to be a dog for a minute. A dog finds food mostly by smell. Sniff each bowl. Which one hides the snack?
flow.kid: Put on the blindfold. Sniff each bowl, one by one. Which one has the snack? Point to it.

ask.q: Was it easy or hard?
good: Hard, my nose is not very strong.
Easy for the banana, hard for the elaichi.

flow.context: This is the first step of Follow Your Nose. You try to find a hidden snack only by smell.

flow.do: Talk about animal noses and other senses.
flow.say: A dog's nose is far, far better than ours. It can follow a smell trail days old. A mosquito finds you by the carbon dioxide you breathe out. A bat finds a moth by its echo. Which sense would help you most to find food in the dark?
flow.kid: A dog could find it at once. A mosquito smells your breath. A bat hears echoes. Which sense would you pick?

check.q: A mosquito finds people in a dark room. Which of these helps it most?
options: Smelling the carbon dioxide we breathe out, and sensing our warmth
Seeing us clearly in the dark
Hearing our hearts beat
check.why: Mosquitoes sense carbon dioxide in breath from a long way off, then use warmth and smell close up. Picking 'seeing clearly' is a natural guess, because we rely on our eyes. But many animals rely on other senses. Picking 'hearts beat' is creative, but heartbeats are far too quiet for a mosquito.

flow.context: This is the step where you compare your nose with animals' senses for finding food.

activities.title: How Long Can a Breath Last?

materials.item: a timer or a clock with a second hand

activities.safety: Do this sitting down, on dry land, never in water. Hold only as long as is comfortable, never until it hurts. Stop at once if you feel dizzy. Children with asthma or heart problems should skip the holding and just do the timing for others.

schedule.what: How Long Can a Breath Last?

activities.record: Write your comfortable breath-hold time and the times of others in the family. Compare them with the animal times on the chart.
activities.context: In this activity, from the founder's Yoga Week, you time how long you can comfortably hold your breath, then compare it with animals that hold their breath to hunt underwater.

setup.art: A child sitting cross-legged on a mat, cheeks gently closed, a grown-up holding a timer.
setup.caption: 1. Sit down. Take a normal breath. Hold it, comfortably.

setup.art: The grown-up writing times in a notebook while a grandparent takes a turn.
setup.caption: 2. Time everyone in the family. Write down the times.

setup.art: A picture chart comparing a child, a Ganges river dolphin, a sea turtle and a deep-diving whale, with clocks.
setup.caption: 3. Compare with animals that hunt underwater.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits cross-legged. 2. They take one normal breath, not a huge one, and hold it. 3. Time how long they hold it comfortably. 4. Stop the moment it feels uncomfortable. 5. Time each family member.
flow.say: Sit tall. Take a normal breath, and hold it gently. Don't push yourself. The moment you want to breathe, breathe. It's not a race to hurt. It's to notice.
flow.kid: Sit tall. Take a normal breath. Hold it gently. Breathe the moment you want to. Never push.
flow.parent: Most children can comfortably hold for 15 to 40 seconds. The urge to breathe comes mostly from carbon dioxide building up in the blood, not from running out of oxygen. Never let this become a contest to hold too long, and never do it in water.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Long Can a Breath Last? You time a comfortable breath-hold, sitting down.

flow.do: Show the chart of animal breath-holds and talk about it.
flow.say: The Ganges river dolphin comes up every minute or two. Some whales stay down for over an hour. How do they do it? They store extra oxygen in their blood and muscles, and slow their hearts down.
flow.kid: Look at the animals. A river dolphin holds its breath for one or two minutes. Some whales hold for over an hour!

chart.title: How long some air-breathing animals often stay underwater

check.q: Ganges river dolphins live in rivers all their lives. Why must they keep coming up?
options: They breathe air with lungs, through a blowhole
They come up to look around
They come up to drink rain
check.why: Dolphins have lungs, not gills. They can only get oxygen from air, through the blowhole on top of the head. Picking 'look around' is a good guess, because Ganges dolphins are nearly blind and find food by echo. But the real reason is breathing.

flow.context: This is the step where you compare your breath-hold with animals that hold their breath to hunt underwater.

activities.title: Mouth Tools Buffet

materials.item: tools: a straw, a tea strainer, a clothes peg, a pair of chopsticks or tweezers, a spoon
foods: a bowl of water or juice, a bowl of water with poha or rice flakes floating in it, a few rubber bands or cooked noodles in a tray of mud or atta, some peanuts

activities.safety: Use clean tools if you plan to eat any food. Don't run with chopsticks or tweezers.
activities.record: Make a table: tool, which food it was best at, and which animal has a mouth like that tool.
activities.context: In this activity you pretend different kitchen tools are animal mouths. You find which tool is best at which food, to see how animal mouths fit the way they get food.

setup.art: A table with a straw, a tea strainer, a clothes peg, chopsticks and a spoon, and bowls of juice, floating poha, noodles in atta and peanuts.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the tool mouths and the foods.

setup.art: A child using a tea strainer to scoop floating poha out of water, like a flamingo.
setup.caption: 2. Try each tool on each food for 30 seconds.

setup.art: A chart with pictures matching the straw to a butterfly, the strainer to a flamingo, chopsticks to a heron and the peg to a parrot.
setup.caption: 3. Match each tool to an animal with that kind of mouth.

flow.do: 1. Set out the foods. 2. Your child tries each tool on each food for 30 seconds. 3. Count how many pieces they collect, or how much juice they drink. 4. Write the best tool for each food.
flow.say: Each tool is a pretend animal mouth. You have 30 seconds with each one. Which mouth is best for which food?
flow.kid: Each tool is an animal mouth. Try each one on each food. You get 30 seconds. Which is best?

ask.q: Which tool was best at the noodles in the atta?
good: The chopsticks or tweezers, like a long beak poking in mud.

ask.q: Which was best at the floating poha?
good: The tea strainer, because the water runs out and the food stays.

flow.context: This is the first step of Mouth Tools Buffet. You try kitchen tools as pretend animal mouths on different foods.

flow.do: Match each tool to an animal and talk about it.
flow.say: Your straw is like a butterfly's long tongue, sipping nectar. The strainer is like a flamingo's beak, sieving tiny food. The chopsticks are like a heron's or a snipe's beak, poking in mud. The peg is like a parrot's strong beak, cracking nuts.
flow.kid: Straw: butterfly. Strainer: flamingo. Chopsticks: heron. Peg: parrot cracking nuts. Which was your favourite?

check.q: A flamingo eats tiny shrimps floating in lake water. In the buffet, which tool worked like its beak?
options: The tea strainer
The straw
The clothes peg
check.why: A flamingo's beak works like a sieve. Water goes out, and tiny food stays in. That's filter feeding. Picking 'the straw' would suck up water and food together, and the flamingo would get mostly water. Picking 'the peg' is good for one big thing at a time, not many tiny ones.

flow.context: This is the step where you match each tool to an animal whose mouth works the same way.

projects.title: My Breath Diary
projects.safety: Count breaths only. Never hold the breath for this project.

schedule.what: Make the diary table. Count breaths for one minute on waking and before bed.
Count breaths on waking, after playing outside, and before bed.
Count breaths while reading, after climbing stairs, and while a grown-up counts yours while you sleep.
Count the breaths of a pet, a sleeping sibling or a grandparent, with permission.
Draw a line chart of your breaths at each time. Write what you found.

projects.record: A table of breath counts at different times of day, and a line chart. Write when you breathed fastest and slowest, and why.
projects.context: In this 5-day project you keep a diary of how many breaths you take in one minute at different times, like waking up, playing and sleeping, and draw a chart.

setup.art: A child sitting up in bed at dawn with a hand on the chest, a small notebook open on the blanket.
setup.caption: 1. Count your breaths for one minute when you wake up.

setup.art: The child sitting on stairs after climbing, panting, a grown-up timing.
setup.caption: 2. Count again after playing or climbing stairs.

setup.art: A notebook with a line chart going up and down across the times of day.
setup.caption: 3. After 5 days, draw a line chart of all your counts.

flow.do: Day 1. 1. Draw a table with columns: day, time, what I was doing, breaths in one minute. 2. Count on waking and before bed.
flow.say: For five days, you'll be a breath scientist. Each day we'll count your breaths at different times. At the end we'll see when you breathe fastest and slowest.
flow.kid: Draw your diary table. Count your breaths when you wake up. Count again before bed.
flow.context: This is the first day of My Breath Diary. You make the table and do the first two counts.

flow.do: Days 2 to 4. Do the day's counts and write them in. On day 3, a grown-up counts the child's breaths while asleep. On day 4, count a pet or another family member.
flow.say: Today's counts are in the diary plan. Remember, sit the same way each time, and count for one whole minute.
flow.kid: Do today's counts. Write each one in your table. Count for one whole minute.
flow.parent: Sleeping breaths are usually slowest. A cat or dog at rest often breathes 20 to 30 times a minute. Small animals breathe faster than big ones.
flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of My Breath Diary. You count your breaths at different times each day.

flow.do: Day 5. 1. Draw a line chart with the times along the bottom and breaths up the side. 2. Write a claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Let's draw a line chart. Each dot is one count. When was the line highest? When was it lowest? Why?
flow.kid: Draw a dot for each count. Join the dots. When was the line highest? Why?

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute during a day
chart.note: Made-up numbers, to show what a chart can look like.

check.q: In the breath diary chart, the line is highest just after climbing stairs. Why?
options: Leg muscles were working hard and needed more oxygen
Stairs have less air
We breathe faster when we are bored
check.why: Hard-working muscles use more oxygen, so you breathe faster to bring more in. Picking 'stairs have less air' mixes this up with high mountains, where air really is thinner. A few stairs make no difference to the air.

flow.context: This is the last day of My Breath Diary. You draw a line chart and explain it.

challenges.title: Design a River-Bottom Hunter
challenges.problem: Imagine a new animal that lives at the bottom of a deep, muddy river, like the Ganga. The water is so brown that it is dark even at noon, and in summer it has very little oxygen. Design an animal that can breathe and find food there.
constraints: Your animal must get enough oxygen, even in summer.
It must find food in water too muddy to see through.
Draw it, label every special part, and say what it eats and how.
materials: clay or play dough, if you want to make a model
pictures of real river animals, if you have them
general: Give it lungs and let it come up to breathe, like the Ganges river dolphin.
Give it gills plus a way to gulp air, like the climbing perch and magur catfish.
Give it whiskers that feel and taste, like a catfish, or echolocation clicks like a dolphin.
creative: The Ganges river dolphin is nearly blind. It swims on its side, sweeping its long beak through the mud, and finds fish with clicks.
Some fish make weak electricity around their bodies and feel when something disturbs it. Could your animal do that?
Could your animal carry an air bubble with it, like the water spiders that live in silk bubbles underwater?
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own river-bottom hunter. Give it a name. Draw it, label it, and explain to your family how it breathes and how it finds food.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You invent an animal that can breathe and find food at the bottom of a dark, muddy river.

setup.art: A cross-section of a brown, murky river with little light reaching the bottom and a few fish in the mud.
setup.caption: 1. Picture the dark, muddy river bottom.

setup.art: A child drawing an invented animal with labels for whiskers, gills and a breathing tube.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your animal. Label its breathing and food-finding parts.

setup.art: The child holding up the drawing and explaining it to a grandparent.
setup.caption: 3. Explain your design to someone.

flow.do: Read the problem with your child and talk about the two problems: little oxygen, and no light.
flow.say: Two problems. One: there isn't much oxygen in the water. Two: it's too dark and muddy to see. What could a body do about each one?
flow.kid: Your animal lives in a dark, muddy river. Two problems: little oxygen, and no light. How could a body solve them?

ask.q: How could it get more oxygen?
good: Come up and breathe air.
Have extra big gills.
Gulp air like the climbing perch.

ask.q: How could it find food in the dark?
good: Smell or taste the water.
Use whiskers.
Use clicks and echoes.

flow.context: This is the first step of Design a River-Bottom Hunter. You think about the two problems your animal must solve.

flow.do: Your child draws the animal and labels each special part.
flow.say: Draw your animal. Label every part that helps it breathe or find food. Then give it a name.
flow.kid: Draw your animal. Label its breathing parts. Label its food-finding parts. Give it a name.

check.q: In a dark, muddy river, which sense would help an animal least to find food?
options: Sharp eyesight
Echolocation clicks
Feeling whiskers
check.why: In water too muddy to see through, eyes don't help much. That's why the Ganges river dolphin's eyes are tiny, and it uses clicks instead. Picking 'echolocation' or 'whiskers' means choosing a sense that works well in the dark, which is a smart choice, but the question asks which helps least.

flow.context: This is the step where you draw and label your river-bottom hunter.

flow.do: Your child explains the design to someone in the family.
flow.say: Tell Nani or a friend about your animal. How does it breathe? How does it find food? What would happen to it if the river got dirtier?
flow.kid: Show your drawing to someone. Explain how it breathes and finds food.
flow.think: Real Ganges river dolphins are in danger. The water is dirtier, and dams block their way. How could people help them?
flow.context: This is the last step of Design a River-Bottom Hunter. You explain your design to someone.

challenges.title: Build a Better Gill
challenges.problem: Tiny bits of food float in water, just as oxygen does. Gills and filter feeders catch what they need from water flowing past. Build a filter that catches as many floating tea leaves as possible from one jug of water poured through it.
constraints: Use one jug of water with one spoon of used tea leaves stirred in.
Pour it through your filter into a bowl in one steady pour.
Count or weigh the tea leaves your filter catches, and compare designs.
materials: a jug of water and a spoon of used tea leaves
filter materials: a cotton handkerchief, a tea strainer, a comb, a sponge, cotton wool, a folded paper towel
a funnel made from a cut plastic bottle
general: A tea strainer catches big leaves but lets tiny bits through.
A cloth catches more, but water flows through slowly.
Several layers catch more than one layer.
creative: Fold the cloth into pleats, like gill threads, to make more surface.
Whale sharks and flamingos use sieves, but gills use thin walls and blood flowing the other way. Can you make water pass slowly over a big surface?
Use two filters one after the other, a coarse one first and a fine one second.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own filter. Draw it, test it, and count how many leaves it catches. Can you beat your best design?
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You build a filter that catches floating tea leaves from water, to see why gills and filter-feeding mouths have lots of surface.

setup.art: A jug of water with used tea leaves swirling in it, next to a funnel made from a cut plastic bottle over a bowl.
setup.caption: 1. Stir used tea leaves into a jug of water.

setup.art: A pleated cotton handkerchief inside the bottle funnel, water being poured through it into a bowl.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the water through your filter.

setup.art: A child counting tea leaves caught on the cloth, spread on a plate.
setup.caption: 3. Count the leaves your filter caught.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the top off a plastic bottle to make a funnel. 2. Stir one spoon of used tea leaves into a jug of water. 3. Try the tea strainer first, as the test to beat.
flow.say: Let's start with the tea strainer. Pour slowly. How many leaves did it catch? How many got through into the bowl?
flow.kid: A grown-up makes a funnel. Pour the tea-leaf water through a tea strainer. How many leaves got through?
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Better Gill. You test a tea strainer as the filter to beat.

flow.do: Your child designs, builds and tests two or three filters, counting the leaves each catches.
flow.say: Now design your own. Think about gills. They're folded into many thin threads to make lots of surface. Can your filter do the same?
flow.kid: Build your own filter. Pour the tea water through. Count the leaves it caught. Try again and make it better.

check.q: In Build a Better Gill, a pleated cloth caught more tea leaves than a flat cloth. Why?
options: Pleats give more surface for the water to pass over
Pleats make the water colder
Pleated cloth is heavier
check.why: Folding the cloth into pleats packs more surface into the same space. More surface catches more. Gills are folded into many thin threads for the same reason. Picking 'colder' or 'heavier' is guessing at other changes. In a fair test, the only thing we changed was the folding.

flow.context: This is the step where you design and test your own filters.

flow.do: Compare the designs. Talk about how real gills differ from filters.
flow.say: Real gills don't trap oxygen like leaves. Oxygen passes through thin walls into blood. But the trick is the same: lots of surface, close to the water.
flow.kid: Which filter won? Real gills also use lots of surface. That's the same trick.
flow.think: A filter catches things. A gill lets oxygen pass through into blood. How are they alike, and how are they different?
flow.context: This is the last step of Build a Better Gill. You compare designs and connect them to real gills.

quiz.p: Why does every animal need oxygen?
opts: Its cells use oxygen to get energy from food
Only to make its blood red
It doesn't. Only land animals need oxygen
quiz.why: Every cell uses oxygen to unlock energy from food. Picking 'only land animals' is a common idea, but fish, crabs and worms need oxygen too. They just get it in different ways.

quiz.p: How does a fish get oxygen?
opts: Water flows in at its mouth, over its gills, and out under the gill covers
It comes to the surface to breathe air, like a dolphin
quiz.why: Fish pump water over their gills, which take oxygen out of the water. Picking 'like a dolphin' mixes up fish and dolphins. Dolphins have lungs and must come up for air.

quiz.p: Lungs, gills and breathing skin are all…
opts: Thin, damp and close to blood
quiz.why: Oxygen can only pass through a thin, wet wall into blood. Picking 'hard and dry' is the opposite. A dry surface can't let oxygen in, which is why fish die out of water and worms die in the sun.

quiz.p: An earthworm is left on a hot, dry path in the sun. Why is that dangerous for it?
opts: Its skin dries out, and it breathes through its skin
It gets sunburned on its gills
It can't see the way home
quiz.why: Earthworms breathe through damp skin. If the skin dries, oxygen can't get through. Picking 'gills' is a mix-up. Earthworms have no gills.

quiz.p: You counted 20 breaths a minute sitting still, and 40 after jumping. What is the best explanation?
opts: Working muscles need more oxygen, so we breathe faster
quiz.why: Muscles working hard use more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide, so we breathe faster. Picking 'timer ran faster' is a good scientist's worry. That's why we used the same timer each time and counted three times.
quiz.context: In the Breath Count experiment, you counted breaths for one minute sitting still, then after jumping.

chart.title: Made-up results: breaths in one minute

quiz.p: In the chuna water test, breathed-out air made the water milky fast. Room air did not. What does this show?
opts: Breathed-out air has more carbon dioxide than room air
quiz.why: Carbon dioxide turns chuna water milky. Breathed-out air carries carbon dioxide from your cells. Picking 'no oxygen' is a common mistake. Breathed-out air still has about 16 parts in 100 oxygen.
quiz.context: In the Chuna Water Test, you bubbled breath into one glass of chuna water and pumped room air into the other.

quiz.p: Which animal finds its food mostly by echoes?
quiz.why: Bats send out high sounds and listen for echoes. Eagles use sharp eyes. Cows graze on grass they can see and smell.

quiz.p: A pit viper hunts mice in the dark. Which special sense helps it?
opts: Pits on its face that sense warmth
Very sharp hearing in big ears
quiz.why: Pit vipers, like the Malabar pit viper of the Western Ghats, have pits that feel the warmth of a mouse. Picking 'echolocation' mixes it up with bats. Snakes don't have outer ears at all.

quiz.p: A vulture eats animals that have already died. What kind of eater is it?
quiz.why: A scavenger eats the dead. Vultures keep the land clean and stop disease from spreading. A filter feeder sieves water. A grazer eats plants.

quiz.p: A spider builds a sticky web and waits. How does it get food?
quiz.why: A web is a trap. Flying insects get stuck, and the spider eats them. Grazing means eating plants for hours. Filtering means sieving water.

quiz.p: Why do earthworms come out onto roads after rain?
opts: Scientists are not sure. There are several ideas
quiz.why: Scientists still argue. Some think the worms need air, some think it's a good time to travel, and some think rain sounds like a hungry mole. Picking a simple answer is natural. But this is a real open question.

quiz.p: Where did the oxygen in the air come from?
opts: Plants on land and tiny algae in the sea made it
It has always been there since the Earth began
quiz.why: Living things that make food from sunlight give out oxygen. More than two billion years ago, tiny ocean living things began filling the air with it. Picking 'always there' is a common idea, but ancient rocks show the early air had almost no oxygen.

quiz.p: Your lungs bring oxygen in. Which parts of you actually use it?
quiz.why: The lungs are like a door. The blood carries oxygen to every cell, from your toes to your brain. Each cell uses it to get energy from food. Picking 'only lungs' is the most common mix-up. Breathing and using oxygen happen in different places.

applications: Doctors count breaths per minute to check if a person is unwell. Fast breathing at rest can be a sign of illness.
Hospitals give oxygen through masks to people whose lungs are not working well.
Divers carry tanks of air because people cannot take oxygen from water.
Fish farmers in India bubble air into ponds in hot weather, so the fish don't run short of oxygen.
Aquarium pumps push air bubbles into fish tanks for the same reason.
Sniffer dogs at airports and with the police find hidden things by smell.
Ships and submarines use sonar, which sends out sounds and listens for echoes, just like bats and dolphins.
Mosquito traps use carbon dioxide or warmth to lure mosquitoes, because that is how mosquitoes find people.
Fish sellers and buyers check bright red gills to see if fish is fresh.
Pranayama and slow breathing are used to calm the body and mind.
Scientists measure the oxygen in rivers to check how healthy the water is for fish.
Engineers copy bird and insect breathing ideas when designing better air filters and machines.

open_questions.q: Why do earthworms crawl onto roads after rain?
open_questions.why_open: There are several ideas: to breathe, to travel, or to escape moles. Experiments support different ideas, and it may be a mix.

open_questions.q: Did lungs come before swim bladders, or swim bladders before lungs?
open_questions.why_open: Most evidence now points to lungs first. But the earliest steps happened over 400 million years ago, and fossils of soft lungs are rare.

open_questions.q: How do deep-diving whales stay underwater for hours without harm?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the tricks, like storing oxygen in muscles and slowing the heart. But whales are hard to study deep in the ocean, so much is still unknown.

open_questions.q: Exactly how does a dog's nose tell apart so many smells?
open_questions.why_open: We know dogs have many more smell cells than us. But how the brain sorts millions of smell mixtures is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Why were some insects giant long ago?
open_questions.why_open: About 300 million years ago there were dragonfly-like insects with wings as wide as a school ruler is long. Some scientists think the air had more oxygen then, which helped insects' air pipes. Others think there were other reasons.

open_questions.q: How do bar-headed geese fly in such thin air?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found that their blood, lungs and hearts are special. But how they manage the hardest climbs is still studied.

open_questions.q: Can people learn to echolocate like bats?
open_questions.why_open: Some blind people use tongue clicks to find their way, and studies show it works. How well people can learn it, and how the brain does it, is still being studied.

maths.problem: You counted your breaths for 15 seconds and got 5. A minute has four lots of 15 seconds. How many breaths would that be in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 seconds, so four lots of 15 seconds. You took 5 breaths in each lot. 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20. Or 4 times 5 is 20.
maths.context: This is about the Breath Count experiment. You count your breaths while sitting still. Counting for a full minute is hard, so you can count for 15 seconds and work out the rest.
maths.why_maths: Counting for a short time and multiplying saves time, and scientists and doctors use this trick to count breaths and heartbeats.

maths.problem: Look at the chart. Sitting still you took 20 breaths a minute. After jumping you took 40. How many times as many breaths did you take after jumping?
maths.explain: After jumping the bar shows 40. Sitting still it shows 20. 40 divided by 20 is 2. So you breathed twice as many times. Check: 20 + 20 = 40.
maths.context: This is about the Breath Count experiment, where you counted breaths sitting still and just after jumping one minute.

chart.title: Made-up results: breaths in one minute

maths.why_maths: Saying 'twice as many' tells us how big the change is, which is more useful than just saying 'more'.

maths.problem: A small fish opened its gill covers 40 times in 30 seconds. How many times would that be in one minute?
maths.explain: One minute is two lots of 30 seconds. 40 + 40 = 80. So the fish opened its gill covers 80 times a minute. That is 4 times as many as a child's 20 breaths.
maths.context: This is about Gill Watch, where you counted how many times a fish's gill covers opened.
maths.why_maths: Turning counts into 'per minute' lets us compare a fish's breathing fairly with our own.

maths.problem: Look at the ant chart. How many ants came to the three baits altogether after 30 minutes? How many more ants were on the sugar than on the salt?
maths.answer: 40 ants altogether. 23 more on the sugar than on the salt.
maths.explain: Sugar 24, biscuit 15 and salt 1. 24 + 15 = 39, and 39 + 1 = 40 altogether. Sugar minus salt is 24 take away 1, which is 23.
maths.context: This is about Ant Detectives. You put sugar, salt and biscuit near an ant path and counted the ants on each after 30 minutes.

chart.title: Made-up results: ants on each bait after 30 minutes

maths.why_maths: Adding up and comparing bars tells us clearly which food the ants liked most, and by how much.

maths.problem: In the breath diary, you breathed 16 times a minute asleep and 34 times a minute after climbing stairs. What is the difference?
maths.explain: 34 take away 16. 34 take away 10 is 24. 24 take away 6 is 18. So you breathed 18 more times a minute after the stairs.
maths.context: This is about My Breath Diary, where you counted your breaths at different times of day for five days.

chart.title: Made-up example: breaths in one minute during a day

maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how much your body changes its breathing to match what you are doing.

roots.context: We have been learning how animals breathe and find food. Now we ask what breathing tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Breathing is not something only lungs do. Every cell breathes, and every breath is a swap with the whole living world.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'lungs' or 'gills' for breathing, and we think the air outside is separate from the body inside. But lungs, gills and skin are only doors. The breathing happens in every cell, and the air in you a moment ago is now outside, on its way to a tree.
deep_truth.evidence: An earthworm has no lungs and breathes through its skin. A fish breathes through gills. They all do the same thing: let oxygen through a thin, damp wall to every cell. And the oxygen itself was breathed out by plants and tiny sea algae.

three.who_am_i: You are millions of millions of breathing cells, working together. Some of their tiny parts were once free-living bacteria.
three.what_is_life: Life is a constant swap. Animals take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide. Plants take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
three.what_is_this_world: The air is shared by everything that breathes. The same air has been in fish, frogs, trees and people.

roots.thread: DeepKids believes that the One shows up as the many. Breathing shows it plainly. There is one need, for oxygen, and it shows up as many doors: lungs, gills, damp skin, tiny air pipes. Behind every door, the same thing happens in every cell. And the air itself is one air, passed from plant to animal to plant, around the whole Earth.

teachings.teaching: Speech, sight, hearing and mind once argued about which of them was the greatest. Each one left the body for a year, and the body carried on. Then breath, prana, began to leave, and all the others were pulled along with it. They agreed that breath was the greatest.
teachings.link: Every animal, whatever its doors, depends on breath first. Without oxygen reaching its cells, no sense and no thought can work.

teachings.source: Kabir, in Robert Bly's version, The Kabir Book (1977)
teachings.teaching: Kabir asks: what is God? And he answers: the breath inside the breath.
teachings.link: Inside each breath is a breath we never feel: oxygen passing into every cell. Kabir points at something even deeper, inside that.

science.text: Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by living things that use sunlight: tiny ocean living things first, more than two billion years ago, then plants. Today, roughly half still comes from algae in the sea.
The tiny energy parts inside our cells, mitochondria, which use the oxygen we breathe, came from bacteria that started living inside bigger cells long ago.

other_view.who: The Charvaka school of ancient India, and many scientists today
other_view.view: Breathing is chemistry: gases passing through walls. It is wonderful, but it needs no One behind it. Body and air are simply different bits of matter meeting. That is an honest view, and it explains breathing well.

practice.title: Ocean breath
practice.say: Let's sit tall and close our eyes. Breathe in slowly through your nose while I count to four. Now breathe out slowly while I count to six, like a soft wave. Again. As you breathe out, imagine your breath going out of the window, to a tree. As you breathe in, imagine the tree's breath coming back to you. Let's do five breaths together. Now open your eyes. Where is your breath now?
